foundations.title: What Is AI, Really?
objectives: Define artificial intelligence, machine learning and deep learning — and see how they nest inside each other
Explain, in plain language, how a neural network learns from data
Understand the two phases every AI goes through: training and inference
Know the key vocabulary: model, parameters, tokens, and neural network
Tell the difference between narrow and general AI, and predictive and generative AI
Understand why AI suddenly exploded in the last few years

sections.h: AI is everywhere — you just stopped noticing
sections.html:
When your phone unlocks by looking at your face, when YouTube lines up the next video you cannot resist, when your keyboard finishes your sentence, when a bank silently blocks a fraudulent transaction — that is artificial intelligence quietly at work. AI is not a distant sci-fi robot. It is already woven into the apps you open a hundred times a day.

Here is an honest, complete definition to build on:

Artificial Intelligence is software that learns patterns from data, and uses those patterns to make predictions or decisions — without a human writing step-by-step instructions for every possible situation.

Notice the key phrase: learns from data. That is what separates modern AI from ordinary software, and it is the idea the rest of this lesson unpacks.

sections.h: The nested dolls: AI, machine learning, deep learning
sections.html:
These three words get used interchangeably, but they actually fit inside one another like Russian dolls.

  • Artificial Intelligence is the big outer goal: machines doing things that normally need human intelligence.
  • Machine Learning (ML) is the main method we use to get there — teaching a system by showing it examples instead of writing rules. Show it thousands of emails labelled "spam" or "not spam," and it learns to sort new ones.
  • Deep Learning is a powerful kind of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. It powers almost everything you have heard of: chatbots, image generators, voice assistants, self-driving cars.
  • Generative AI is the newest layer inside deep learning — models that produce brand-new text, images, code, and audio from human prompts.

AI, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI — nested, not interchangeable.

So every chatbot is deep learning, which is machine learning, which is AI. But a simple rule-based thermostat can be "AI" without any learning at all. The word is broad — now you can be precise about which kind you mean.

sections.h: How a neural network actually learns
sections.html:
A neural network is loosely inspired by the brain. It is made of thousands or millions of tiny units ("neurons") connected together. Each connection has a number called a weight that says how strongly one unit pushes on the next.

Learning works like this, and it is simpler than it sounds:

  1. Show the network an example (say, a photo) and let it guess the answer ("cat" or "not cat").
  2. Compare its guess to the correct answer. The size of the mistake is called the loss.
  3. Nudge every weight a tiny bit in the direction that would have reduced the mistake.
  4. Repeat this millions of times, with millions of examples.

Slowly, the weights settle into values that capture the real pattern — what "cat-ness" looks like. Nobody programmed the rules for whiskers or ears; the network discovered them by adjusting numbers until it stopped being wrong.

🔍 Deeper dive: what "parameters" really are

Those adjustable weights are called parameters — think of them as tiny dials. When you hear a model has "70 billion parameters," it means 70 billion dials were tuned during training. The automatic tuning process is called gradient descent: it is like finding the bottom of a valley in fog by always stepping downhill. More parameters, more data, and more downhill steps generally mean a smarter model.

sections.h: Training vs. using it: the two phases
sections.html:
Every AI lives two very different lives.

  • Training is the school years — slow, expensive, done once. The model sees enormous amounts of data and tunes its parameters. Training a large model can cost millions of dollars and use warehouses of computers.
  • Inference is the working life — fast and cheap. This is the moment you type a question and it answers. The parameters are now frozen; it is simply applying what it already learned.

This is why a chatbot answers instantly but sometimes does not know recent news: its expensive "school years" ended on a certain date, and everything after that is outside what it studied.

sections.h: How a chatbot 'thinks' — and what a token is
sections.html:
A chatbot like the one that helped build this course is a large language model (LLM). Here is the surprising truth: at its core, it is a spectacularly good next-word predictor. Given the words so far, it predicts the most likely next piece of text, then the next, then the next — one step at a time — until the answer is complete.

It does not work in whole words, but in tokens — small chunks of text. "Unbelievable" might be three tokens: "un", "believ", "able". The model juggles probabilities over tens of thousands of possible tokens at every single step. Do that fast enough, over enough knowledge, and the result feels like understanding.

But remember what is really happening: it is pattern-based prediction, not a conscious mind with beliefs or feelings. Holding onto that one fact will make you wiser about AI than most adults.

sections.h: Two useful maps: narrow vs. general, predictive vs. generative
sections.html:
Two simple distinctions will help you classify any AI you meet.

  • Narrow AI is brilliant at one thing — translating, recommending, recognising faces. Every AI that exists today is narrow. General AI (AGI) — a system as flexible as a human across any task — does not yet exist, despite the headlines.
  • Predictive AI classifies or forecasts: spam or not, this disease or that, tomorrow's demand. Generative AI creates something new: text, images, audio, video. The generative wave is what made AI famous, and it is what you will use in the next four lessons.

AI ideas are decades old, so why did everything change so suddenly? Three ingredients finally arrived at once:

  1. Data — the internet created oceans of text and images to learn from.
  2. Computing power — specialised chips (GPUs) made it possible to tune billions of parameters.
  3. A breakthrough design — in 2017 a new neural-network architecture called the transformer made language models dramatically better at handling context. Almost every modern chatbot is built on it.

When data, compute and the transformer met, AI leapt from "interesting" to "world-changing" in just a few years — right as you were growing up alongside it.

activity.title: Try it yourself: See the learning happen
activity.text: Open any chatbot and ask: "Explain how you were trained, in simple terms, and what a parameter is." Then ask a follow-up: "What is something you cannot know because of when your training ended?" Notice how the answers line up with this lesson — you now understand the machine well enough to interrogate it.

takeaways: AI contains machine learning, which contains deep learning (neural networks) — nested dolls
Neural networks learn by adjusting millions of 'dials' (parameters) to reduce their mistakes
Every model has two phases: expensive training, then fast, frozen inference
A chatbot predicts text one token at a time — powerful pattern prediction, not consciousness
Today's AI is all narrow; data + compute + the 2017 transformer caused the recent explosion

quiz.q: How do machine-learning systems mainly gain their abilities?
opts: A programmer writes a rule for every case
They adjust internal parameters to reduce mistakes on many examples
They copy answers from a fixed list
They are manufactured already knowing everything
quiz.fb: Learning = tuning parameters (weights) over many examples until the errors shrink. No hand-written rules for each case.

quiz.q: A model's 'parameters' are best described as…
opts: Millions of adjustable dials tuned during training
quiz.fb: Parameters are the tunable weights. '70 billion parameters' means 70 billion dials were set during training.

quiz.q: Why can a chatbot answer instantly but not know last week's news?
opts: Answering is 'inference' (fast); its expensive 'training' ended on a past date
quiz.fb: Training is the one-time, costly learning phase; inference is fast use of frozen knowledge — so anything after the training cutoff is unknown.

quiz.q: Which statement is true today?
opts: General AI (as flexible as a human) is already common
All current AI is 'narrow' — great at specific tasks
quiz.fb: Every AI in use today is narrow. General AI does not yet exist, and current systems are not conscious.

foundations.title: Talking to AI: The Art & Science of Prompting
foundations.summary: Turn any AI into an expert on demand
objectives: Understand what a prompt is and why it controls the quality of every answer
Use a repeatable framework — Role, Task, Context, Format, Constraints — to structure prompts
Apply named techniques: zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought prompting
Understand the 'context window' and why long conversations sometimes drift
Diagnose and fix a weak prompt like a professional

sections.h: The prompt is the steering wheel
sections.html:
A prompt is simply what you type to an AI. Here is the secret almost nobody is taught: the quality of your prompt decides the quality of your answer. The same model can hand you something useless or something brilliant — and the difference is usually you, not the machine.

This is a genuine, in-demand skill. Employers now list "prompting" and "working with AI" on job adverts. Learning it well is, for this decade, what knowing how to search Google was for the last one — except the payoff is far larger.

A large model has absorbed an enormous amount of the world's writing. Buried inside it are the patterns of a tutor, a lawyer, a poet, a coder, a coach. Your prompt does not teach it those things — it selects which of them to bring forward. A vague prompt lands you in the bland middle of everything it knows. A precise prompt steers it to the exact corner you need.

🔍 Deeper dive: the context window

Everything in your current conversation — your prompt, pasted text, and the AI's replies — sits in a working memory called the context window, measured in tokens. It is large but finite. In very long chats the earliest details can fall out of view, which is why the AI sometimes "forgets" what you said at the start. Fix: restate key details, or start fresh for a new task.

sections.h: The anatomy of a strong prompt: R-T-C-F-C
sections.html:
Great prompts are not luck. Most contain five ingredients. You will not need all five every time, but keep the checklist in mind:

  • Role — who the AI should be. "Act as a patient physics tutor."
  • Task — exactly what you want done. "Explain acceleration."
  • Context — your situation. "I am a Grade 10 student in Nepal preparing for exams and I find formulas confusing."
  • Format — the shape of the answer. "Give me three short points, then one worked example."
  • Constraints — the limits. "Use simple words, under 200 words, no advanced maths."

Stack these together and an ordinary request becomes a precise brief the model can nail on the first try.

sections.h: Three named techniques the pros use
sections.html:
Beyond the checklist, three techniques have real names and real power:

  1. Zero-shot — you just ask, with no examples. Fine for simple tasks.
  2. Few-shot — you give two or three examples of what "good" looks like, then ask for more of the same. Perfect for matching a style or format: paste three strong CV bullet points and say "write four more like these."
  3. Chain-of-thought — you add "think step by step" or "show your reasoning before the final answer." For maths, logic and multi-step problems this dramatically improves accuracy, because it forces the model to work through the steps instead of blurting a guess.

sections.h: Weak prompt to strong prompt: a live upgrade
sections.html:
Weak: "Help me with history."

Strong: "Act as a friendly history tutor (role). I am a Grade 9 student who struggles to remember dates (context). Explain the three main causes of World War One (task) in simple language, then give me a memory trick for each (format). Keep it under 250 words (constraint)."

Same tool. A completely different result. That single example contains the whole skill.

sections.h: Iterate — the first answer is a draft, not a verdict
sections.html: Amateurs accept the first reply. Professionals treat it as round one and steer: "make it shorter," "add a real-world example," "explain the second point more simply," "now turn it into five flashcards." Each nudge sharpens the result. The willingness to go three or four rounds is what separates people who get gold from AI and people who give up and call it useless.

activity.title: Try it yourself: The five-ingredient rewrite
activity.text: Pick something you genuinely need help with this week. Write the laziest one-line prompt for it. Now rewrite it using all five ingredients — Role, Task, Context, Format, Constraints — and add "think step by step" if it involves reasoning. Run both. The gap between the two answers is the value of this lesson.

takeaways: The prompt controls the result; it 'aims' the model at the expertise you need
Structure prompts with Role, Task, Context, Format and Constraints
Use few-shot (give examples) for style, and chain-of-thought ('think step by step') for reasoning
The context window is finite — restate key details in long chats or start fresh
Iterate: treat the first answer as a draft and keep steering

quiz.q: Which prompt is strongest?
opts: 'Act as a biology tutor. I'm a Grade 8 student who finds diagrams confusing. Explain how the heart pumps blood in 4 simple steps, then give one everyday analogy.'
quiz.fb: It carries role, context, task, format and a constraint — the full R-T-C-F-C recipe.

quiz.q: 'Chain-of-thought' prompting means…
opts: Sending many prompts in a chain
Asking the AI to reason step by step before answering
quiz.fb: Asking it to 'think step by step' improves accuracy on maths and logic by forcing it to work through the steps.

quiz.q: You want answers to match a very specific style. Best technique?
opts: Few-shot: give 2–3 examples of the style, then ask for more
quiz.fb: Few-shot prompting — show examples of 'good' — is the fastest way to lock in a style or format.

quiz.q: Why can an AI seem to 'forget' details from early in a long chat?
opts: Early details can fall out of the finite context window
It deletes your messages on purpose
quiz.fb: The context window (working memory) is large but limited; in long chats, restate key details or start fresh.

foundations.title: Creating with AI: Images, Video, Audio & Code
objectives: Map the main types of generative tools — image, video, audio, voice, and code
Explain, in plain language, how text-to-image tools turn words into pictures (diffusion)
Write a professional image prompt using subject, style, composition, lighting and detail
Understand negative prompts, seeds and iteration
Reason clearly about copyright, deepfakes and the ethics of AI creation

sections.html: You can now describe something in plain language and watch AI create it: a poster, an illustration, a logo, a voice-over, a short video, a melody, even working computer code. A single student with a laptop can produce what once needed a whole studio and a budget. This is genuinely new in human history — and you get to grow up fluent in it.

• Text → Image: describe a picture, get artwork in seconds — posters, projects, concept art, logos.
  • Text → Video: describe a scene, get a short animated clip. Newer and rougher, but improving fast.
  • Text → Audio & Voice: generate music, sound effects, or a natural-sounding narrator.
  • Image → Image: upload a sketch or photo and have AI restyle, extend or edit it.
  • Text → Code: describe a program and get working code — a huge productivity boost for anyone learning to build things.

These tools learned from hundreds of millions of image-and-caption pairs, so they connect words to visual patterns. The clever part is how they draw, a process called diffusion:

  1. During training, the model repeatedly takes a real image and adds random visual "noise" until it is pure static — and learns to reverse each step.
  2. When you give a prompt, it starts from pure noise and removes it step by step, always steering toward what your words describe.

Out of static, guided by your text, an image gradually emerges. You do not need the mathematics — you need to recognise that it is the same big idea from Lesson 1: patterns learned from data, applied to something new.

sections.h: The anatomy of a great image prompt
sections.html:
Weak image prompts give one or two words. Strong ones layer five elements:

  • Subject — what it is: "a red panda reading a book."
  • Style — the look: "soft watercolour illustration."
  • Composition — the framing: "close-up, centred, sitting under a tree."
  • Lighting & mood — "warm evening light, cosy and calm."
  • Detail & quality — "highly detailed, gentle textures."

Two more professional tools: a negative prompt tells it what to avoid ("no text, no blur"), and a seed is the starting random pattern — keep the same seed to make small tweaks without changing everything, or change it to explore fresh variations.

sections.h: The ethics you must not skip
sections.html:
AI creation raises real, unsettled questions. Be the person who asks them:

  • Whose work trained this? Models learned from human artists. Should those artists be credited or paid? Courts and companies are still deciding.
  • Who owns the output? The law on whether an AI image can be copyrighted — and by whom — is genuinely grey and varies by country.
  • Is it honest? Entering AI art in a hand-drawn competition, or passing AI work off as your own, is deception. Always disclose when something is AI-made.
  • Could it harm? The same tools that fake a fun image can fake a damaging one of a real person. Power demands responsibility.

activity.title: Try it yourself: The five-layer image brief
activity.text: Write one image prompt for a poster promoting your school's science fair, using all five layers — subject + style + composition + lighting + detail — and add a short negative prompt. If you can access an image tool, generate it, then change just one word (say, the lighting) and regenerate. Watch how a single word reshapes the whole picture.

takeaways: Generative tools now span image, video, audio/voice, image-editing and code
Text-to-image works by diffusion: start from noise and remove it, steered by the meaning of your words
Strong image prompts layer subject, style, composition, lighting and detail — plus negative prompts and seeds
Video and voice extend the same pattern-learning idea, which is why they are powerful and easy to misuse
Always disclose AI-made work and think about artists, ownership and potential harm

quiz.q: Text-to-image tools mainly create pictures by…
opts: Starting from random noise and removing it step by step toward your description
Searching the web for a match
quiz.fb: That guided denoising is diffusion — combining learned concepts into something new, not copying a file.

quiz.q: A 'negative prompt' is used to…
opts: Tell the tool what to leave out of the image
Make the image black and white
quiz.fb: Negative prompts specify what to avoid, e.g. 'no text, no blur' — a key professional control.

quiz.q: A strong image prompt usually layers…
quiz.fb: Layering these five elements gives the tool everything it needs to aim the result precisely.

quiz.q: The responsible way to share AI-made art is to…
opts: Pretend you drew it by hand
Be honest it's AI-made and consider artists, ownership and harm
quiz.fb: Disclosure and ethical awareness are the marks of a responsible creator.

foundations.title: AI as Your Study Partner
foundations.summary: Learn faster, and actually remember it
objectives: Use AI to power proven learning methods: active recall, spaced repetition and the Feynman technique
Climb Bloom's levels of thinking — from remembering to creating — with AI's help
Build a personal study system: practice tests, flashcards and study plans on demand
Understand the integrity line between learning with AI and cheating yourself
Run a simple verification workflow so you never trust a wrong answer

sections.h: The most patient tutor you will ever have
sections.html: Stuck on a concept at 11pm? AI never tires, never judges, never runs out of patience. Used well, it is the most available tutor in the world. The entire skill is using it to build understanding, not to skip understanding. This lesson shows you how — using methods that learning scientists have proven actually work.

Decades of research agree on what makes learning stick. AI can drive each one on demand:

  • Active recall — testing yourself beats re-reading. Prompt: "Quiz me on this chapter, one question at a time, and tell me if I'm right before the next."
  • Spaced repetition — reviewing at growing intervals fights forgetting. Prompt: "Turn my mistakes into flashcards and make a 7-day review schedule."
  • The Feynman technique — you understand something only when you can explain it simply. Prompt: "I'll explain photosynthesis to you like you're 10. Point out anything I got wrong or left out."

Learning is not one thing — there are levels. Bloom's famous ladder runs from basic to advanced thinking, and you can prompt AI to help at every rung:

  1. Remember: "List the key terms in this chapter with one-line definitions."
  2. Understand: "Explain the main idea using an analogy from football."
  3. Apply: "Give me a new problem that uses this formula, then check my solution."
  4. Analyse: "Compare these two causes of the war — which was more important, and why?"
  5. Evaluate: "Here's my argument. What is its weakest point?"
  6. Create: "Help me design an experiment to test this idea."

Most students only ever use AI at the bottom rung. Climbing higher is where real learning — and better grades — live.

Combine the above into a repeatable routine you can run before any exam:

  • Diagnose: "Ask me five questions to find what I don't understand about this topic."
  • Explain the gaps: "Explain the ones I got wrong, simply, with an example each."
  • Practise: "Generate a 10-question practice test at exam difficulty, then mark it and explain my errors."
  • Plan: "Build me a realistic 2-week revision plan for these three subjects, 1 hour a day."

sections.h: The line you must not cross
sections.html:
Here is the honest rule. Asking AI to explain something so you can understand it and do the work yourself is learning. Asking AI to do the assignment so you can hand it in as your own is cheating — and worse, you learn nothing, which shows up in the exam hall where no chatbot exists.

Think of AI as a coach, never a ghostwriter. A coach drills you until you are stronger; a ghostwriter leaves you weak and dependent.

activity.title: Try it yourself: The tutor flip
activity.text: Pick the topic you find hardest right now. Run the full loop: ask an AI to quiz you (five questions, one at a time, checking each), then ask it to turn your wrong answers into flashcards with a review schedule. Finally, explain the topic back to it and let it catch your gaps.

takeaways: AI can power active recall, spaced repetition and the Feynman technique on demand
Testing yourself beats re-reading — struggling to recall strengthens memory (the testing effect)
Use Bloom's ladder to push past 'remember' into apply, analyse, evaluate and create
Explaining and practising = learning; handing in AI's work = cheating yourself
Verify anything important — AI can be confidently wrong

quiz.q: Which study method does research say is most effective?
opts: Active recall — testing yourself on the material
quiz.fb: The 'testing effect': struggling to retrieve answers strengthens memory far more than re-reading.

quiz.q: Using AI at the 'analyse' or 'create' level of Bloom's ladder means…
opts: Comparing ideas, critiquing arguments, or designing something new with its help
quiz.fb: Most students stay at 'remember'. Real learning happens higher up — analysing, evaluating and creating.

quiz.q: Which use of AI is genuine learning, not cheating?
opts: Submitting an AI-written essay as your own
Having it explain a concept so you can then do the work yourself
Copying its answer onto your exam
quiz.fb: Understanding with AI's help, then doing the work yourself, is learning. Handing in its work teaches you nothing.

quiz.q: 'Productive struggle' means…
opts: Wrestling with a problem before seeing the answer, which builds understanding
quiz.fb: Some difficulty is desirable — it's what makes learning stick. Letting AI remove all struggle removes the learning.

foundations.title: Being Smart & Safe with AI
objectives: Explain why AI hallucinates and where it is most dangerous
Understand how bias enters AI systems, with real examples
Recognise deepfakes and defend yourself against AI-driven misinformation
Protect your privacy and personal data when using AI tools
Understand how AI is made safer (guardrails, RLHF) — and why it is still imperfect
See how AI will reshape careers, and which human skills keep you ahead

sections.html: You have seen what AI can do. Now the most important lesson of all: how to use it wisely. Powerful tools reward the people who understand their limits and quietly punish those who don't. This lesson is your defence kit.

Remember Lesson 1: a chatbot predicts plausible text, not true text. Most of the time plausible and true line up — but not always. When they diverge, the model can produce a hallucination: a confident, fluent, completely made-up "fact," fake quote, or fake source.

Hallucinations are most dangerous exactly where you are least able to catch them: niche topics, specific numbers, citations, recent events, and anything local the model barely saw in training. The defence is simple: verify anything that matters.

AI can now fake realistic photos, voices and videos of real people — deepfakes. A convincing fake video of a leader, a friend, or you can be made from a handful of samples. This changes a basic rule of life: seeing is no longer believing.

  • Check the source — who posted it, and is it reported by trusted outlets?
  • Look for confirmation — real events show up in many independent places.
  • Pause before sharing — misinformation spreads because people react fast.

sections.h: Privacy: your data is the price
sections.html:
Whatever you type into a public AI tool may be stored and used to improve future models. Treat the chat box like a postcard, not a diary. Practical rules:

  • Never paste passwords, ID numbers, bank details, or private information.
  • Be careful with schoolwork or personal writing you would not want stored.
  • Check the tool's settings to turn off training or delete history.

Make this your reflex with any AI output. Four questions:

  1. Could this be wrong? (hallucination)
  2. Where did it come from, and can I confirm it? (sources)
  3. Who might this be unfair to? (bias)
  4. Would I be comfortable if everyone knew I used AI here? (honesty)

activity.title: Try it yourself: Catch the hallucination
activity.text: Ask an AI a detailed factual question about your own town, school, or a small local topic it is unlikely to know well. Study the answer for anything invented or slightly off, then verify it against a real source. You have just practised the single most important safety skill: catching a confident mistake before you trust it.

takeaways: Hallucinations happen because AI predicts plausible text, not true text — verify what matters
Bias enters through training data and can be magnified at scale — stay alert to unequal treatment
Deepfakes mean 'seeing is no longer believing' — check sources and pause before sharing
Never give public AI tools your passwords or private data; check the privacy settings
Safety training (RLHF, guardrails) helps but is imperfect — your critical thinking is the final layer
Your edge in an AI world is judgement, creativity, ethics, communication and adaptability

quiz.q: Why do AI chatbots sometimes 'hallucinate'?
opts: They are infected by a virus
They predict plausible-sounding text, which is not always true
They copy Wikipedia word for word
quiz.fb: A model predicts what usually comes next, not what is true — so it can be confidently, fluently wrong.

quiz.q: Where does AI bias mainly come from?
opts: The AI choosing to be unfair
Patterns in the human data it was trained on
quiz.fb: Bias reflects the training data — and can be magnified when a model is used by millions.

quiz.q: The safest habit with public AI tools is to…
opts: Paste your passwords so it remembers you
Never enter passwords or private personal data, and check the settings
Type your bank PIN for convenience
quiz.fb: Treat the chat box like a postcard. Keep passwords and private data out, and use privacy settings.

quiz.q: What gives a person the real edge in an AI-powered future?
opts: Pairing AI's speed with human judgement, creativity and adaptability
Memorising more facts than the AI
quiz.fb: AI handles speed and scale; your judgement, creativity, ethics and adaptability are what keep you ahead.

healthcare.title: AI Foundations for Healthcare
healthcare.summary: The concepts and vocabulary every clinician now needs
objectives: Distinguish artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI — and know where each belongs in clinical practice
Explain how a model learns from data, in language you could use with a colleague or a patient
Interpret the performance measures that actually matter clinically: sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value, and AUC
Understand why a model's accuracy depends entirely on the population it was trained on
Recognise the difference between a research result and a clinically deployable tool

sections.h: Why this matters to you, now
sections.html:
Artificial intelligence has moved out of the research literature and into the consulting room. Ambient documentation tools are drafting clinical notes. Algorithms are reading chest X-rays for tuberculosis in district hospitals. Patients are arriving at appointments having already consulted a chatbot about their symptoms.

That last point deserves attention. OpenAI reports that more than 5% of all ChatGPT messages globally are about healthcare — billions of messages each week — and that roughly one in four of its 800 million weekly users asks a health question every week. Whatever your institution decides about AI, your patients have already decided about it.

This programme is not about turning clinicians into data scientists. It is about giving healthcare professionals the vocabulary, judgement and critical instincts to evaluate these tools, use the good ones well, and refuse the bad ones with confidence.

These words are used interchangeably in vendor brochures. Precision protects your patients.

  • Artificial Intelligence (AI) — the broad field of systems performing tasks that normally require human intelligence. A rules-based drug-interaction alert in your prescribing system is AI, with no learning involved.
  • Machine Learning (ML) — systems that learn patterns from data rather than following rules a person wrote. Nearly all clinical prediction models are machine learning.
  • Deep Learning — machine learning using multi-layered neural networks. It is what made medical image interpretation possible: radiographs, retinal photographs, histopathology slides, dermatoscopic images.
  • Generative AI — models that produce new content: text, images, summaries. This is the large-language-model wave now entering clinical documentation and patient communication (Module 5).

A useful clinical translation: deep learning looks at things (images, signals, waveforms); machine learning predicts events (deterioration, readmission, mortality); generative AI writes things (notes, summaries, letters). Each carries a very different risk profile and a different regulatory expectation.

sections.h: How a model learns — without the mathematics
sections.html:
A neural network contains many simple units connected together, each connection carrying a number called a weight. Learning proceeds like this:

  1. Show the model a case — say, a chest radiograph — and let it predict the label ("TB" or "not TB").
  2. Compare its prediction to the confirmed answer. The size of the error is called the loss.
  3. Adjust every weight slightly in the direction that would have reduced the error.
  4. Repeat across tens or hundreds of thousands of labelled cases.

Gradually the weights settle into a configuration that captures real radiographic patterns. Nobody programmed a rule for cavitation or upper-lobe infiltrate; the model derived the pattern statistically from examples.

This has a profound clinical implication. The model knows only what its training data contained. A model trained on radiographs from well-resourced European hospitals has never seen the film quality, the patient demographics, or the disease prevalence of a district hospital in Nepal. Its published accuracy does not travel with it.

Deeper dive: what "parameters" means when a vendor says it

Those adjustable weights are the model's parameters. A modern imaging model may have tens of millions; a large language model may have tens of billions. More parameters allow more complex patterns, but also demand more data and make the model harder to interpret. Parameter count is a specification, not a measure of clinical usefulness — never accept it as evidence of quality.

sections.h: Reading performance like a clinician, not a customer
sections.html:
You already have the mental model for this: it is the same reasoning you apply to any diagnostic test.

  • Sensitivity — of patients who truly have the condition, what proportion does the model identify? Low sensitivity means missed disease.
  • Specificity — of patients without the condition, what proportion does it correctly clear? Low specificity means false alarms, unnecessary investigation, and patient anxiety.
  • Positive predictive value (PPV) — of those flagged positive, how many truly have it? PPV depends on prevalence, so a model with excellent PPV in a high-prevalence referral centre may perform poorly in a low-prevalence screening population.
  • Negative predictive value (NPV) — of those cleared, how many are genuinely disease-free? Critical when a model is used to rule out.
  • AUC / c-statistic — overall discrimination across all thresholds. 0.5 is a coin toss; 1.0 is perfect. It is a useful summary but tells you nothing about performance at the threshold you will actually use.

Two questions separate an informed buyer from a naive one. First: "At what threshold, and what are the sensitivity and specificity there?" Second: "What was the disease prevalence in the validation population, and how does it compare with mine?" A vendor who cannot answer both is selling you a research artefact.

sections.h: Accuracy is a property of a population, not of a model
sections.html:
This is the single most important idea in the module. Sensitivity and specificity are relatively stable properties of a test; predictive values are not — they shift with prevalence. A tuberculosis screening algorithm validated where prevalence is 15% will generate a very different burden of false positives where prevalence is 0.5%.

The same logic applies to every other axis of difference: age distribution, comorbidity, imaging equipment, staining protocol, skin tone, sex, nutritional status. When any of these differ between the training population and yours, published performance is a hypothesis about your setting — not a fact about it.

An enormous gap separates a promising paper from a safe clinical tool. The World Economic Forum notes that more than 70% of US FDA approvals in this space have centred on imaging applications, most of which have yet to be implemented at scale. Regulatory clearance is not the same as clinical adoption, and clinical adoption is not the same as demonstrated patient benefit.

Before a tool touches a patient, four questions must all be answered:

  1. Was it validated externally — on data from institutions that did not contribute to training?
  2. Was it validated prospectively — on patients as they actually present, not on a curated retrospective set?
  3. Does it change decisions — and do those changed decisions improve outcomes?
  4. Does it work here — in this population, with this equipment, in this workflow?

Most published models fail at question one.

• It is not clinical reasoning. It is pattern recognition. It has no model of physiology, no concept of the patient in front of you, and no awareness of what it does not know.
  • It is not objective. A model trained on historical clinical decisions inherits historical clinical patterns, including inequitable ones.
  • It is not stable over time. Populations change, protocols change, equipment changes. Performance degrades silently — a phenomenon called dataset shift, covered in Module 6.
  • It is not accountable. Under every framework that currently exists, the registered health professional remains responsible for the clinical decision.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the question that reframes any demonstration
practitioner.text: When a vendor demonstrates a diagnostic tool, ask: "Which hospitals contributed the training data, and what were the patient demographics and disease prevalence?" If the answer is a well-resourced tertiary centre in a high-income country and your setting is a district hospital in South Asia, treat the quoted accuracy as unproven in your context until you validate it locally. Performance is not portable.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Take one diagnostic or triage decision made repeatedly in your department. Write down: (a) the outcome an algorithm would need to predict, (b) roughly what proportion of your patients have that outcome (the prevalence), and (c) which error would harm the patient more — a missed case or a false alarm. Your answer to (c) determines the threshold the tool should be set at, and that is a clinical decision, not a technical one.

takeaways: Deep learning interprets images; machine learning predicts events; generative AI produces text — different risks, different governance
A model learns statistical patterns from its training data and knows nothing beyond them
Judge tools on sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV at the operating threshold — not on AUC or accuracy alone
Predictive values shift with prevalence, so performance does not transfer between populations
Regulatory clearance is not evidence of patient benefit; external and prospective validation are what matter
The registered health professional remains accountable for every clinical decision

quiz.q: A tuberculosis screening algorithm reports 94% accuracy. Before accepting this, your most important question is:
opts: "What were the sensitivity, specificity and disease prevalence in the validation population?"
"How many parameters does the model have?"
quiz.fb: Accuracy is nearly meaningless without knowing the threshold performance and the prevalence of the validation population — predictive values shift with prevalence.

quiz.q: A model is used to RULE OUT a serious condition. Which measure matters most?
quiz.fb: To safely rule out disease you need high sensitivity and high negative predictive value — otherwise cases are missed and falsely reassured.

quiz.q: Why may a model validated in a European tertiary centre underperform in a Nepali district hospital?
opts: Differences in patient population, disease prevalence, equipment and image quality mean performance does not transfer
quiz.fb: Model performance is a property of the population and conditions it was trained and validated on — it must be revalidated locally.

quiz.q: 'Dataset shift' describes:
opts: Silent degradation of model performance as populations, protocols or equipment change over time
quiz.fb: Dataset shift is gradual and produces no error message — which is precisely why ongoing monitoring is mandatory.

quiz.q: Which statement about accountability is correct under current frameworks?
opts: The registered health professional remains accountable for the clinical decision
No one is accountable when AI is involved
The AI vendor is legally responsible for clinical outcomes
Accountability transfers to the hospital's IT department
quiz.fb: AI is a decision-support tool. Clinical and legal accountability continues to rest with the responsible health professional.

healthcare.title: Health Data: The Foundation and the Bottleneck
healthcare.summary: Why data quality decides whether clinical AI succeeds or fails
objectives: Explain why data quality — not algorithm sophistication — determines the success of clinical AI
Identify the data realities of health systems in Nepal and comparable settings: paper records, fragmented systems, incomplete registries
Understand labelling, ground truth and why they are harder in medicine than in any other domain
Recognise class imbalance, data leakage and unrepresentative training data
Understand interoperability standards and why they determine what is possible
Apply privacy and consent principles to health data used for AI

sections.h: The uncomfortable truth about clinical AI projects
sections.html:
Across industries, roughly a quarter of organisations report extracting meaningful value from generative AI, according to BCG — and healthcare providers sit close to that benchmark at around 29%. The reason so many initiatives stall is rarely the algorithm. It is the data underneath it.

Healthcare has a specific problem the technology industry underestimates: medicine's ground truth is genuinely uncertain. In most domains the label is obvious — a transaction was fraudulent or it was not. In medicine, two experienced radiologists may disagree on the same film. The "correct answer" a model learns from is itself a human judgement with its own error rate.

sections.h: Where health data actually lives in a typical system
sections.html:
• Paper case notes and registers — still the primary clinical record in many facilities, particularly at district and primary level.
  • Hospital information systems — often covering admissions, billing and pharmacy but not clinical detail.
  • Laboratory and imaging systems — frequently standalone, with results returned as printed reports or PDF images rather than structured data.
  • Vertical programme systems — separate registries for tuberculosis, HIV, immunisation, maternal health, each with its own identifiers.
  • Community health worker records — often paper-based, held at the community level and aggregated only in summary.

To train a model predicting, say, treatment outcome in tuberculosis, you must link a patient's presentation, radiograph, laboratory confirmation, treatment record and final outcome — data that may sit in five systems with no shared patient identifier. When the linkage fails silently, the resulting dataset is quietly wrong, and no amount of modelling sophistication will rescue it.

sections.h: Labelling and ground truth: medicine's hardest problem
sections.html:
Supervised learning requires labelled examples. In healthcare, obtaining that label is expensive and often ambiguous.

  • Expert time is scarce. Labelling ten thousand radiographs requires radiologist hours that most systems cannot spare.
  • Experts disagree. Inter-observer variation is a well-documented reality in radiology, pathology and dermatology. A model trained on one reader's labels learns that reader's idiosyncrasies.
  • The best label may arrive late. Confirmed diagnosis may only emerge after culture results, biopsy or clinical course — sometimes months later.
  • Proxy labels mislead. Using "was treated for X" as a proxy for "had X" encodes clinical decision-making patterns, including the tendency to under-investigate certain patient groups.

Deeper dive: why proxy labels are dangerous in health equity terms

If a model is trained to predict "patients who received specialist referral" as a proxy for "patients who needed specialist referral," it will faithfully reproduce whatever referral inequities already exist. Groups historically under-referred will be predicted to need less care — and the model will appear to perform well, because it accurately predicts what happened. This is one of the most consequential and least visible errors in clinical AI.

sections.h: Three technical traps with clinical consequences
sections.html:
• Class imbalance. Serious outcomes are usually rare. A model predicting in-hospital mortality where mortality is 2% can achieve 98% accuracy by predicting survival for everyone — and be clinically useless. Always ask for sensitivity and PPV, never accuracy.
  • Data leakage. Information that would not exist at the moment of decision creeps into training. A sepsis model that includes "antibiotics administered" appears extraordinary and fails immediately in prospective use, because at the moment of prediction that field is empty. The test: would this value genuinely exist, in this form, at the moment the clinician needs the prediction?
  • Unrepresentative training data. If a dermatology model was trained overwhelmingly on lighter skin tones, its performance on darker skin may be substantially worse. If a model was trained only on adults, it should not be used in paediatrics. Representation is a safety issue, not a diversity gesture.

sections.h: Interoperability: the standards that decide what is possible
sections.html:
Two standards dominate:

  • HL7 FHIR — the modern standard for exchanging structured clinical data between systems.
  • DICOM — the universal standard for medical imaging, which is why imaging AI has advanced faster than almost any other clinical application: the data was already standardised.

This is not a technical footnote. It is strategy. The World Economic Forum urges health systems to move "from fighting on infrastructure to winning on services" — prioritising shared digital public infrastructure rather than each institution building its own incompatible stack. For a country still building its digital health foundations, choosing interoperable standards now is far cheaper than retrofitting them later.

sections.h: Privacy, consent and the special status of health data
sections.html:
Health data attracts the strictest protection in nearly every legal system, and for good reason: it is intimate, permanent, and capable of causing discrimination in employment, insurance and social standing.

Practical obligations that apply regardless of jurisdiction:

  • Lawful basis and consent — patients must understand how their data may be used, including for developing or improving AI.
  • De-identification is not absolute. Removing names is insufficient; rare diagnoses, precise dates and geography can re-identify individuals. Imaging carries particular risk — facial reconstruction from head CT and MRI is demonstrably possible.
  • Purpose limitation — data collected for clinical care cannot be silently repurposed for commercial model development.
  • Cross-border transfer — sending patient data to an overseas cloud service is a governance decision requiring explicit assessment, not an IT convenience.
  • Data sovereignty — the WEF frames the goal as "local control of data within a globally connected and patient-centred system."

Nepal's Privacy Act (2075) and associated regulations, together with institutional research ethics requirements, govern this domain locally. Always confirm current requirements with your institution's ethics committee or legal adviser before any data leaves clinical control.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the linkage test
practitioner.text: Before endorsing any AI proposal in your institution, ask a single question: "Can we reliably link this patient's record across the systems this model needs, using a consistent identifier?" If the answer is no, the first project is not AI — it is patient identification and record linkage. That is unglamorous, but it is the foundation everything else stands on, and it delivers value even if no model is ever built.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Choose one clinical question in your department that AI might help with. List every data element a model would need. Mark each as: (A) reliably recorded in digital form today, (B) recorded but on paper or in a separate system, (C) not captured at all. Then ask: who would provide the labels, and how confident are we that those labels are correct? This is the honest feasibility assessment most proposals skip.

takeaways: Clinical AI projects fail on data far more often than on algorithms
Ground truth in medicine is itself uncertain — experts disagree, and labels are expensive and often delayed
Proxy labels reproduce existing inequities while appearing to perform well
Class imbalance makes accuracy meaningless; leakage produces spectacular but fake performance
Unrepresentative training data is a patient-safety issue
FHIR and DICOM interoperability determine what is buildable; shared infrastructure beats fragmented systems
Health data demands the strictest privacy discipline — de-identification alone is not protection

quiz.q: A sepsis prediction model includes 'broad-spectrum antibiotics administered' as an input and performs extraordinarily well. What is wrong?
opts: The antibiotics should be weighted lower
Data leakage: that information does not exist at the moment the prediction is needed
Nothing — antibiotics are a valid predictor
quiz.fb: Antibiotic administration follows the clinical suspicion of sepsis. Including it leaks the outcome into the prediction — impressive in testing, useless prospectively.

quiz.q: A model trained to predict 'patients who received specialist referral' as a proxy for clinical need will most likely:
opts: Reproduce existing referral inequities while appearing to perform well
Improve access for under-served groups automatically
quiz.fb: Proxy labels encode historical decision patterns. Groups previously under-referred will be predicted to need less care — and the model will look accurate.

quiz.q: Why has imaging AI advanced faster than most other clinical applications?
opts: Imaging data was already standardised through DICOM
quiz.fb: DICOM gave imaging a universal standard long before other clinical data was structured, making large training datasets feasible.

quiz.q: Removing patient names from a dataset before sharing it:
opts: Is insufficient — rare diagnoses, dates, geography and imaging can enable re-identification
quiz.fb: De-identification is a spectrum, not a guarantee. Head imaging in particular carries demonstrated re-identification risk.

quiz.q: In a population where an outcome occurs in 2% of patients, a model reporting 98% accuracy:
opts: May be predicting 'no' for everyone and be clinically useless
quiz.fb: Severe class imbalance makes accuracy misleading. Sensitivity, PPV and the clinical cost of each error type are what matter.

healthcare.title: AI in Diagnosis & Clinical Decision Support
healthcare.summary: Imaging, triage, early warning and the limits of the evidence
objectives: Map where AI is genuinely established in diagnosis today and where claims outrun evidence
Understand medical imaging AI: radiology, pathology, ophthalmology and dermatology
Understand clinical deterioration and early-warning models, and why they often disappoint
Apply the concepts of assistive, autonomous and triage modes of deployment
Evaluate explainability tools and understand their real limits
Integrate AI output into clinical reasoning without succumbing to automation bias

sections.html:
AI in diagnosis is not uniformly mature. Evidence is strongest where the input is a standardised image, the question is narrow and binary, and large labelled datasets exist:

  • Diabetic retinopathy screening from retinal photographs — among the most validated applications, with several systems approved for use in screening programmes internationally.
  • Tuberculosis screening from chest radiographs — of direct relevance to Nepal and much of South Asia, and covered in detail in Module 4.
  • Mammography and lung nodule detection — well studied, increasingly deployed as a second reader.
  • Histopathology — detection and grading tasks on digitised slides.
  • Stroke imaging triage — flagging large-vessel occlusion to accelerate time-critical pathways.

Evidence is considerably weaker for broad diagnostic reasoning across undifferentiated presentations — precisely the task clinicians find hardest and where a tool would be most valuable. Be sceptical of any product claiming general diagnostic capability.

sections.h: Three modes of deployment — and why the distinction matters
sections.html:
The same algorithm carries entirely different risk depending on how it is used:

  • Assistive. The model offers a second opinion; a clinician reads independently and decides. Lowest risk, and the appropriate default. The main hazard is automation bias.
  • Triage or prioritisation. The model reorders the worklist so urgent cases are read first, but every case is still read by a human. This is often the highest value-to-risk ratio in a resource-constrained system — nothing is missed that would otherwise have been caught, and time-critical findings surface sooner.
  • Autonomous. The model issues a result without human review. Appropriate only in narrowly defined, heavily validated, regulator-approved circumstances, and requiring explicit clinical governance and a clear safety net for the cases it clears.

When evaluating a proposal, establish which mode is intended before discussing anything else. Many disagreements about clinical AI dissolve once this is clarified.

Predicting which ward patient will deteriorate is enormously attractive — and historically disappointing. Well-documented problems in the literature include poor external validity when models move between institutions, alarm burden that produces fatigue and dismissal, and models that predict deterioration only marginally earlier than an attentive nurse.

The lesson is not that these models are useless, but that the intervention matters more than the prediction. A prediction that does not trigger a defined, resourced clinical response changes nothing. Before deploying any early-warning system, agree exactly what happens when it fires, who responds, and within what time — and measure whether that response actually occurs.

Deep learning models are not directly interpretable, so several techniques attempt to explain their outputs:

  • Saliency and heat maps highlight image regions that most influenced the output. Genuinely useful for spotting gross errors — a model attending to a scanner artefact or a laterality marker rather than pathology.
  • SHAP and similar methods quantify each variable's contribution to an individual prediction, which suits tabular clinical models.
  • Case-based explanation shows similar training examples, which clinicians often find more intuitive than either of the above.

The honest caveat

A heat map shows where the model looked, not why it concluded what it concluded. It can create a comfortable but false sense of understanding. Explainability tools are quality-assurance instruments for catching obvious failures — they are not a substitute for external validation, and they should never be the primary evidence that a model is safe.

sections.h: Automation bias: the clinical risk you are most likely to underestimate
sections.html:
Automation bias is the documented human tendency to accept a machine recommendation even when independent evidence contradicts it. In clinical settings this cuts both ways: clinicians may over-call findings the model flags, and — more dangerously — may under-call findings the model missed.

The effect is strongest in exactly the conditions where AI is most deployed: high volume, time pressure, fatigue, and junior staff working beyond their comfort zone. It is also self-reinforcing, because a model that is usually right trains you to stop checking.

Practical mitigations that have some support in practice:

  • Read before you look. Where feasible, form your own impression before revealing the AI output.
  • Treat disagreement as a signal to slow down, not as a prompt to defer.
  • Track override rates. If clinicians almost never disagree with the model, that is a governance warning, not a success metric.
  • Preserve the right to disagree without administrative penalty, and record the reasoning.

sections.h: How to appraise a clinical AI study
sections.html:
You already know how to appraise a diagnostic accuracy study. Apply the same rigour, plus four AI-specific questions:

  1. Was validation external and prospective? Retrospective internal validation is the weakest evidence and the most commonly reported.
  2. What was the comparator? "Better than a junior trainee" and "better than an experienced consultant" are very different claims.
  3. Were failure cases published? A study reporting no analysis of errors is incomplete.
  4. Was any patient outcome measured — or only diagnostic concordance? Improved detection that does not change management or outcome is not yet clinical value.

Reporting guidelines now exist for AI studies — including the CONSORT-AI and SPIRIT-AI extensions for trials and STARD-AI for diagnostic accuracy — and are a reasonable benchmark to expect from any serious vendor evidence pack.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: start with triage, not autonomy
practitioner.text: In a resource-constrained service, the safest and highest-value first deployment is almost always worklist prioritisation. Every study is still read by a human, so nothing can be missed that would otherwise have been caught — but urgent findings surface hours or days earlier. The clinical benefit is real, the risk profile is modest, and it builds institutional confidence before anything more ambitious is attempted.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Identify one imaging or test-reporting backlog in your institution. Estimate the current time from acquisition to clinical action. Then specify what a triage-mode AI would need to achieve to be worth adopting: what sensitivity would you require, what would happen to a flagged case, who would act, and how would you measure whether time-to-action actually improved? You have just written a deployable evaluation protocol.

takeaways: Evidence is strongest for narrow, image-based, binary tasks — weakest for broad diagnostic reasoning
Assistive, triage and autonomous deployment carry very different risks; clarify the mode first
A prediction without a defined, resourced clinical response changes nothing
Heat maps show where a model looked, not why it decided — explainability is QA, not proof of safety
Automation bias is strongest under fatigue and time pressure; low override rates are a warning sign
Demand external, prospective validation and outcome measures — not retrospective concordance

quiz.q: Which deployment mode generally offers the best value-to-risk ratio for a first clinical AI project in a busy, under-resourced service?
opts: Triage or worklist prioritisation, with every case still read by a human
quiz.fb: Triage surfaces urgent findings sooner while a human still reviews everything, so nothing can be missed that would otherwise have been caught.

quiz.q: An early-warning model accurately predicts deterioration but outcomes do not improve. The most likely explanation is:
opts: No defined, resourced clinical response was attached to the alert
quiz.fb: Prediction without a specified, staffed intervention changes nothing. Define who responds, how, and within what time — then measure it.

quiz.q: A saliency heat map over a chest radiograph tells you:
opts: Which image regions most influenced the output — useful for catching gross errors, but not a causal explanation
Why the model reached its conclusion
That the model is safe to deploy
quiz.fb: Heat maps localise influence, not reasoning. They are a quality-assurance tool, not evidence of safety.

quiz.q: Clinicians in your department almost never disagree with the AI's output. This is:
opts: A governance warning sign suggesting possible automation bias
quiz.fb: Near-zero override rates suggest deference rather than independent judgement — a hallmark of automation bias.

quiz.q: Which is the strongest form of evidence for a diagnostic AI tool?
opts: High AUC on the training set
External, prospective validation with patient outcome measures
quiz.fb: External and prospective validation, ideally with outcomes rather than concordance alone, is the standard to demand.

healthcare.title: AI in Practice: Real-World Use Cases Today
healthcare.summary: What is actually deployed and improving patient care right now
objectives: Describe concrete, documented deployments of AI improving patient care today
Identify which of these are directly relevant and transferable to Nepal and similar health systems
Understand what made each deployment work — and what limited it
Distinguish genuinely operational applications from pilots and marketing claims
Build a realistic picture of what your own institution could implement within twelve months

sections.html:
Every example below is drawn from documented deployments or published research reported in the sources for this programme. For each, we note what it does, what evidence supports it, and — most importantly for our purposes — how transferable it is to a resource-constrained setting.

A caution before we begin. The gap between "demonstrated in a study" and "working reliably in a district hospital" is wide. The World Economic Forum observes that although more than 70% of FDA approvals in this field concern imaging, most have yet to be implemented at scale. Read what follows as evidence of what is possible, not as a procurement list.

What it does. Computer-aided detection software analyses a chest radiograph and returns an abnormality score indicating the likelihood of tuberculosis, allowing triage of who needs confirmatory molecular testing.

The evidence. The UNDP background paper on AI in developing-country health systems documents pilot studies of the Delft Institute's CAD4TB software for computer-aided diagnosis of pulmonary tuberculosis from chest radiographs in Tanzania and Zambia, where performance compared well with that of human experts. WHO has separately examined AI-supported radiograph interpretation as a triage and screening tool in high-burden settings.

Why it matters here. This is arguably the single most relevant clinical AI application for Nepal. Tuberculosis remains a major public health burden across South Asia; chest radiography is widely available even at district level; and the binding constraint is not equipment but the availability of someone qualified to interpret the film promptly. An algorithm that triages radiographs so that likely-positive cases reach molecular testing faster addresses a genuine bottleneck rather than an imagined one.

Limits. Performance varies with population, prevalence and image quality, and requires local threshold-setting. It is a triage tool, not a diagnosis — bacteriological confirmation remains essential.

What it does. Software analyses retinal photographs to identify referable diabetic retinopathy, allowing screening to occur without an ophthalmologist reading every image.

The evidence. The UNDP paper cites work by Bellemo and colleagues deploying AI for diabetic retinopathy screening in Zambia, which showed clinically acceptable performance in detecting referable disease when compared with human assessment. This is among the most extensively validated applications of clinical AI globally.

Why it matters here. Diabetes prevalence is rising rapidly across South Asia. Retinopathy is asymptomatic until late, is detectable, and is treatable — the classic profile of a condition where screening saves sight. The constraint everywhere is ophthalmologist time. A screening programme where trained technicians capture images and AI triages them extends specialist reach dramatically.

Limits. Requires a functioning referral pathway. Screening that identifies disease no one can treat is not a service — it is an audit of your own inaccessibility. Build the treatment pathway first.

sections.h: 3. Detecting birth asphyxia from an infant's cry
sections.html:
What it does. Ubenwa, developed in Nigeria and documented in the UNDP paper, applies signal processing and machine learning to the sound of a newborn's cry to help identify birth asphyxia in low-resource settings.

Why it matters here. This example is worth dwelling on because it demonstrates a principle that matters more than any single product: the most transferable innovations are those designed for constraint from the outset. It requires no imaging, no laboratory, no reliable electricity — only a microphone. Birth asphyxia is a leading contributor to neonatal mortality, and the settings where it is most lethal are precisely those with no specialist present at delivery.

The lesson. Solutions built in high-resource settings and exported downward often fail. Solutions built for low-resource settings frequently transfer both ways. When scanning for what to adopt, look first at what was designed for conditions resembling yours.

What it does. The system listens to the clinical encounter and drafts the note, which the clinician reviews, edits and signs.

The evidence. BCG's outlook on digital health reports that electronic health records increasingly incorporate ambient AI scribes that record and summarise patient conversations, reducing the time physicians spend documenting encounters, drafting notes and responding to messages — with the stated benefit that a lighter administrative load returns time to patient care.

Why it matters. Documentation burden is a leading driver of clinician burnout worldwide, and burnout is a workforce-retention issue in systems that can least afford to lose staff. This is one of the few applications where the primary beneficiary is the clinician, which is also why adoption tends to be enthusiastic rather than resisted.

Limits for our setting. Current tools are optimised for English and a handful of major languages, and assume reliable connectivity and an electronic record to write into. Multilingual consultations — routine in Nepal — remain a genuine technical challenge. This is an application to watch closely rather than adopt immediately, and a strong candidate for local language development.

sections.h: 5. Patients using AI to navigate care — already happening
sections.html:
What is happening. OpenAI's analysis of anonymised usage reports that healthcare accounts for more than 5% of all ChatGPT messages globally, that around one in four weekly users asks a health question each week, and that more than 40 million people ask health questions daily. Strikingly, seven in ten health conversations occur outside normal clinic hours, and users in underserved rural areas send roughly 600,000 healthcare-related messages weekly.

A documented case. The report describes a user in San Francisco who used ChatGPT to help coordinate urgent care for her mother in Indonesia after sudden vision loss the family had attributed to fatigue. The model warned that the presentation could signal a hypertensive crisis and possible stroke; the family measured her blood pressure, which confirmed the concern, and she was admitted. The guidance was subsequently confirmed by a doctor in Indonesia, and her vision substantially recovered.

Why this matters to you. Note what actually happened: AI did not diagnose or treat. It escalated appropriately and got the patient to a clinician faster. That is the realistic and genuinely valuable role for consumer AI in health — triage and navigation, particularly where distance, cost or hours delay presentation.

The clinical implication you cannot ignore

Patients are arriving having already consulted AI. Dismissing this is neither realistic nor helpful. The constructive response is to ask what they were told, correct it where it is wrong, and use it as an opening for shared decision-making. OpenAI's own observation is instructive: reliability improves when answers are grounded in the right patient-specific context — which is precisely what you, and not the chatbot, possess.

sections.h: 6. Telemedicine, triage and reaching the unreached
sections.html:
What it does. Intelligent triage systems assess presenting symptoms and route patients to the appropriate level of care, escalating urgent cases. KPMG's work with FICCI in India describes AI transforming remote care and telemedicine by enabling continuous monitoring and ensuring timely escalation of cases.

Why it matters here. Nepal's geography makes this compelling. Where a patient is a day's travel from a district hospital, the decision of whether to travel is itself a high-stakes clinical judgement — usually made with no clinical input. AI-supported triage delivered through a health worker's phone can improve that decision without requiring the patient to move.

Limits. Triage tools inherit the safety profile of their thresholds. Set them to minimise unnecessary travel and you will miss cases; set them to catch everything and you will overwhelm referral centres. This calibration is a health-system policy decision, not a vendor setting.

sections.h: 7. Public health surveillance and programme management
sections.html:
What it does. Predictive models analyse routine surveillance data to detect outbreak signals earlier, forecast demand, and target interventions geographically.

The evidence and framing. The KPMG–FICCI paper describes AI enhancing disease surveillance, optimising resource allocation and enabling targeted interventions for non-communicable diseases and maternal and child health, alongside fraud detection and monitoring in public health schemes. The WEF similarly identifies public health surveillance and resource allocation as core public-sector applications.

Why it matters here. This may be the highest-leverage application for a ministry of health, because it operates on data that already exists in routine reporting systems and does not require new devices at the point of care. It is also where weak data quality bites hardest — the output can only be as good as the completeness and timeliness of routine reporting.

sections.h: 8. Drug discovery and the science pipeline
sections.html:
What it does. AI accelerates target identification, molecular design and clinical trial planning. The UNDP paper notes DeepMind's AlphaFold reliably predicting three-dimensional protein structures — a genuine scientific milestone — and the use of AI to identify potential treatments for Ebola virus disease.

Why it matters here — with an important caveat. Nepal is unlikely to conduct frontier drug discovery. But the UNDP paper raises a question that matters enormously for developing countries: how appropriate is it for a small number of private actors to control intellectual property for technologies with the potential to be public goods, particularly where the underlying research was publicly funded? In developing-country settings, access may be constrained by restrictive licensing rather than by science. That is a policy conversation your health leadership should be part of.

sections.h: 9. Hospital operations and the administrative layer
sections.html:
What it does. Scheduling optimisation, bed and theatre management, supply chain and inventory forecasting, claims and billing automation, and patient engagement platforms. KPMG India documents deployments including AI-powered patient engagement systems in large multispecialty hospitals and generative-AI conversational platforms operating across hospital chains with location-specific responses.

Why it matters here. This is the least glamorous category and frequently the most immediately valuable. It carries lower clinical risk, produces measurable results quickly, and builds institutional confidence and data discipline before anything touches a diagnosis. For most hospitals, this is where a sensible AI programme starts.

sections.h: What these examples have in common
sections.html:
Across every successful deployment above, four features recur:

  1. They address a real bottleneck — a shortage of interpreters, of specialist time, of access — rather than demonstrating a capability.
  2. They keep a human in the decision loop, with AI triaging, drafting or prioritising rather than concluding.
  3. They fit an existing workflow and existing infrastructure, rather than requiring the workflow to be rebuilt around them.
  4. They connect to an actionable pathway. Detection without treatment capacity is not a service.

Any proposal you are shown that lacks all four deserves careful scepticism, however impressive the technology.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: pick the bottleneck, not the technology
practitioner.text: The most reliable way to choose a first project is to ignore technology entirely for an hour. Ask instead: where do patients in our service wait longest, travel furthest, or get missed most often — and why? Then ask whether any of the applications in this module addresses that specific cause. Projects chosen this way survive; projects chosen because a tool was impressive rarely do.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Choose the ONE example from this module most relevant to your institution. Write half a page covering: the specific bottleneck it would address; roughly how many patients are affected each month; what data and equipment you already have; what the referral or treatment pathway would be for a positive finding; and what single measure would tell you within six months whether it worked. Keep this — it becomes the core of your capstone proposal in Module 9.

takeaways: TB radiograph triage and diabetic retinopathy screening are the most directly relevant validated applications for Nepal
Ubenwa shows that tools designed for constrained settings transfer better than tools exported downward
Ambient AI scribes address clinician burnout but currently assume English and reliable connectivity
Patients already use AI for health — seven in ten such conversations happen outside clinic hours
Consumer AI's realistic value is escalation and navigation, not diagnosis
Operations and surveillance applications often deliver faster, safer value than clinical tools
Successful deployments address a real bottleneck, keep humans deciding, fit the workflow, and connect to an actionable pathway

quiz.q: Which application is most directly relevant to Nepal's disease burden and existing infrastructure?
opts: Genomic newborn screening at population scale
AI triage of chest radiographs for tuberculosis
quiz.fb: Chest radiography is widely available; the constraint is timely expert interpretation. TB triage addresses a genuine bottleneck with existing equipment.

quiz.q: The Ubenwa example from Nigeria illustrates which principle?
opts: Tools designed for low-resource constraints from the outset transfer better than tools exported downward
Neonatal care cannot benefit from AI
Audio analysis is superior to imaging
Only wealthy countries can build useful AI
quiz.fb: Requiring only a microphone, it was designed for the constraints it serves — which is why it transfers. Imported high-resource solutions frequently fail.

quiz.q: Before launching a retinopathy screening programme, the most important prerequisite is:
opts: A functioning referral and treatment pathway for positive findings
quiz.fb: Screening that detects disease no one can treat is not a service. Build the treatment pathway before the detection capability.

quiz.q: In the documented case where AI helped a family in Indonesia, what did the AI actually contribute?
opts: It escalated appropriately, prompting urgent assessment that led to hospital admission
It diagnosed and treated the condition
quiz.fb: The realistic and valuable role of consumer AI in health is triage and navigation — getting the patient to a clinician faster, not replacing one.

quiz.q: For most hospitals, the safest place to begin an AI programme is:
opts: Operational and administrative applications such as scheduling and documentation
quiz.fb: Operational applications carry lower clinical risk, deliver measurable results quickly, and build the data discipline and confidence needed for clinical work later.

quiz.q: Detection capability without treatment capacity amounts to:
opts: An audit of your own inaccessibility rather than a service
quiz.fb: Identifying disease you cannot treat does not improve outcomes and may erode trust. The pathway matters as much as the detection.

healthcare.title: Generative AI in Clinical Practice
healthcare.summary: Documentation, communication and safe professional use of language models
objectives: Understand what a large language model is and how it differs from a clinical prediction model
Identify high-value generative AI applications in clinical and administrative work
Explain retrieval-augmented generation and why it is the safe pattern for clinical knowledge tools
Write effective prompts for clinical and academic tasks
Know exactly what must never be entered into a public AI tool
Design human review proportionate to clinical risk

sections.h: A different technology, a different failure mode
sections.html:
The models in Modules 3 and 4 output a probability. A large language model (LLM) outputs text, generated by repeatedly predicting the next fragment of language.

The clinical consequence is critical. A diagnostic model can be wrong in ways you can measure and monitor. A language model can be wrong fluently, confidently and plausibly — producing a well-structured paragraph containing a fabricated drug interaction, an invented guideline recommendation, or a citation to a paper that does not exist. This is hallucination, and in medicine it is the defining safety problem of generative AI.

The danger is amplified by presentation. Fluent, confident, correctly formatted clinical prose reads as authoritative. Your instinct for detecting an unreliable source — hesitancy, poor grammar, vagueness — does not fire.

The strongest applications share a shape: language-heavy, high-volume, and verifiable by a competent professional.

  • Clinical documentation. Drafting notes, discharge summaries, referral letters and operation notes for clinician review.
  • Patient communication. Translating discharge instructions into plain language, and into the patient's own language — of real significance in a multilingual country.
  • Guideline and protocol lookup. Answering "what does our protocol say about X?" with citations to your institution's approved documents.
  • Literature synthesis. Summarising evidence for a journal club, teaching session or audit — with sources verified.
  • Administrative correspondence. Insurance documentation, referral paperwork, committee minutes.
  • Coding support. Suggesting diagnostic and procedure codes from a clinical narrative for human confirmation.
  • Teaching and assessment. Generating case vignettes and examination questions for faculty review.
