Notice that most of these are administrative and communicative rather than diagnostic. That is where the risk-adjusted value currently sits.

sections.h: Retrieval-augmented generation: the safe clinical pattern
sections.html:
A general language model answers from its training data, which does not include your hospital's formulary, your national treatment protocols, or this year's guideline revision. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) corrects this:

  1. Your approved documents — protocols, formulary, national guidelines — are indexed.
  2. A question first triggers a search of that indexed content.
  3. The retrieved passages are given to the model with an instruction to answer only from them.
  4. The answer is returned with citations to the source document and section.

Three properties make this the appropriate architecture for clinical knowledge tools: answers reflect your approved practice rather than generic or foreign guidance; hallucination is substantially constrained; and every answer is checkable. When a vendor offers a clinical assistant, the first question is whether it is grounded in your documents and whether it cites them.

Deeper dive: production-grade retrieval is harder than it looks

BCG cautions that real-world retrieval systems are not off-the-shelf components. Clinical documents contain tables, dosing charts, algorithms and cross-references that naive text-chunking destroys — and a dosing table split across two chunks can produce a confidently wrong answer. Ask any vendor specifically how their system handles tables, figures and document structure, and test it against your own protocols before trusting it.

sections.h: Prompting for clinical and academic work
sections.html:
Output quality tracks instruction quality. A dependable structure:

  • Role — "You are assisting a physician preparing a discharge summary."
  • Task — "Summarise this admission."
  • Source — "Use only the clinical notes provided below."
  • Format — "Structure as: presenting complaint, course, procedures, discharge medications, follow-up."
  • Constraints — "Do not infer any diagnosis, dose or finding not explicitly documented. Where information is missing, write MISSING rather than estimating."

That last constraint is the clinical professional's habit and it deserves emphasis. Instructing the model to flag gaps rather than fill them converts its most dangerous tendency into a safety feature. A summary containing three "MISSING" markers is far safer than one that quietly invented three plausible values.

Two further techniques: ask for reasoning before conclusions on analytical tasks, and supply two or three examples when you need output matched to a house format.

sections.h: What must never be entered into a public AI tool
sections.html:
Text entered into a public consumer AI service may be stored and, depending on the provider and settings, used to improve future models. With health data this is a serious breach of confidentiality and, in most jurisdictions, of law.

Never enter into a public tool:

  • Patient names, hospital numbers, national ID numbers, addresses or contact details
  • Dates of birth, admission or procedure combined with any other identifying detail
  • Clinical narratives containing identifiable information — including rare diagnoses that identify a person in a small community
  • Photographs, scans or documents containing patient identifiers or faces
  • Staff personal data, or unpublished institutional or research data

Legitimate alternatives: an enterprise deployment with contractual guarantees that data is not retained for training; a private or on-premise deployment; or rigorous de-identification before use. Every institution should hold a written, circulated acceptable-use policy. If yours does not, that is a concrete and immediate action from this module.

The realistic risk in most hospitals

The greatest exposure is not a sophisticated attack. It is a tired junior doctor at 2am pasting a patient's clinical summary into a free chatbot to help draft a discharge letter — with no intent to do harm and no idea a policy was breached. This is addressed by clear guidance and accessible approved alternatives, not by disciplinary action after the fact.

• Low risk — light review. Internal meeting notes, teaching material drafts, literature summaries for personal use.
  • Medium risk — substantive review by a competent professional. Referral letters, patient information leaflets, translated instructions, coding suggestions.
  • High risk — full verification against source, plus second review. Anything entering the medical record; anything stating a diagnosis, dose or contraindication; anything given directly to a patient.
  • Not appropriate without specific institutional governance — autonomous clinical advice to patients without clinician review, or unreviewed AI-generated content entering the record.

The accountability principle is unchanged and worth stating plainly to your teams: the professional who signs the note owns the note. "The AI wrote it" is not a defence to a patient, a coroner, or a regulator.

One application deserves particular attention in our context. Modern language models handle Nepali and other South Asian languages far better than earlier systems, which creates a genuine opportunity: discharge instructions, medication guidance and consent materials produced in the language the patient actually speaks.

The equity gain is real — comprehension drives adherence, and adherence drives outcomes. But two cautions apply. Translation quality is materially better for widely written languages than for those with less digital text, so performance across Nepal's languages will be uneven. And clinical translation must be verified by a competent speaker before it reaches a patient. A confidently mistranslated dosing instruction is a patient-safety event.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the MISSING rule
practitioner.text: Add one line to every clinical prompt you write: "Where information is not explicitly present in the source, write MISSING — do not infer or estimate." This single instruction converts the model's most dangerous habit into a visible safety signal, and it takes two seconds. Teach it to every junior member of your team as their first lesson in using these tools.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Take one document your team produces repeatedly — a discharge summary, a referral letter, patient instructions. Write a complete prompt using Role, Task, Source, Format and Constraints, including the MISSING rule. Then define the review step: who verifies it, against what source, before it enters the record or reaches the patient. Finally, identify which approved tool your institution actually permits for this — and if none exists, that is your finding.

takeaways: Language models fail fluently and confidently — hallucination is the core clinical safety problem
Best current value is documentation, communication and administration, not diagnosis
RAG grounds answers in your own approved protocols and provides citations — demand it and test it on tables
Structure prompts with Role, Task, Source, Format and Constraints, and always include the MISSING rule
Patient-identifiable information must never enter a public AI tool; provide an approved alternative
Scale review to risk; the professional who signs the note owns the note
Translation offers real equity gains but must be verified by a competent speaker

quiz.q: Why is retrieval-augmented generation the preferred architecture for a clinical knowledge assistant?
opts: It removes the need for clinician review
It grounds answers in your own approved protocols and provides checkable citations
quiz.fb: RAG retrieves your authoritative content first, constraining hallucination and making every answer traceable to a source.

quiz.q: Which prompt instruction most directly reduces the risk of fabricated clinical detail?
opts: "Where information is not explicitly present in the source, write MISSING — do not infer."
quiz.fb: Instructing the model to flag gaps rather than fill them converts its most dangerous tendency into a visible safety signal.

quiz.q: A junior doctor pastes a patient's clinical summary into a free public chatbot to draft a discharge letter. This is:
opts: Acceptable if the patient is not named in the first line
Fine if the chat is deleted afterwards
A breach of patient confidentiality and likely of data protection law
quiz.fb: Public tools may retain and train on submitted text. Identifiable clinical information must never be entered — and institutions must provide an approved alternative.

quiz.q: Which task requires the HIGHEST level of verification?
opts: AI-drafted content entering the medical record or stating a dose
Generating a teaching case for faculty review
Summarising a journal article for personal reading
quiz.fb: Anything entering the record or specifying a diagnosis, dose or contraindication requires full verification against source plus second review.

quiz.q: AI-generated translation of discharge instructions into a patient's language should be:
opts: Verified by a competent speaker before it reaches the patient
Given directly to the patient to save time
quiz.fb: The equity benefit is real, but a confidently mistranslated dosing instruction is a patient-safety event. Verification is mandatory.

healthcare.title: The Dangers: Risks of AI in Healthcare
healthcare.summary: Patient safety, bias, privacy and the risks that matter clinically
objectives: Apply a structured taxonomy of AI risk specific to clinical care
Understand how AI can cause direct patient harm, and through which mechanisms
Recognise algorithmic bias as a health-equity and patient-safety issue
Understand dataset shift, silent failure and why monitoring is mandatory
Assess privacy, cybersecurity and third-party risks in a clinical context
Understand deskilling, liability and the risk of widening the digital divide

sections.h: Why this module carries more weight in medicine
sections.html:
In most industries an AI failure is a financial or reputational event. In healthcare it can be a death. That single fact should shape how every professional in this programme evaluates these tools.

The World Economic Forum is direct about the tension: health is "inherently sensitive... leading to a highly risk-averse environment," compounded by public scepticism toward AI. That caution is legitimate and protective. The purpose of this module is not to discourage adoption but to ensure adoption is safe, and survivable when something goes wrong — because eventually something will.

• False negatives. Missed disease. A screening tool that fails to flag a malignancy, particularly where it has replaced rather than supplemented human review.
  • False positives. Unnecessary investigation, invasive procedures, treatment toxicity, and genuine psychological harm. In screening programmes this is the dominant harm at scale.
  • Hallucinated clinical content. A fabricated dose, interaction or guideline recommendation that reads authoritatively (Module 5).
  • Alert fatigue. Excessive alerting causes clinicians to dismiss alerts reflexively — including the true ones. A system that over-alerts can reduce safety below the no-system baseline.
  • Workflow harm. A tool that adds clicks, delays discharge or fragments attention can worsen care even when its predictions are accurate.
  • Inappropriate autonomy. Deploying in autonomous mode a model validated only for assistive use.

sections.h: 2. Algorithmic bias — a safety issue, not a compliance issue
sections.html:
AI learns from historical clinical data, and historical clinical data reflects historical inequities in access, investigation and treatment. Three mechanisms recur:

  • Under-representation in training data. If a population was scarce in the training set, performance for that population is unproven and often worse — by skin tone, sex, age, body habitus, ethnicity or comorbidity.
  • Proxy labels. As covered in Module 2, training on "who received care" rather than "who needed care" faithfully reproduces existing inequity while appearing accurate.
  • Measurement bias. Where the underlying measurement performs differently across groups, any model built on it inherits that distortion.

Three features make algorithmic bias more dangerous than individual clinician bias: it is invisible without deliberate testing, it is systematic — applied identically to every patient rather than varying by clinician — and it compounds, because under-served groups generate less data and so remain poorly modelled.

The equity stake for developing countries

The UNDP background paper warns plainly that "it is challenging to take disruptive technology innovations from developed countries and replicate them to address the unique needs of the developing world." A tool trained on populations unlike yours may not merely underperform — it may systematically underperform for your patients while carrying published accuracy figures that suggest otherwise. Local validation is not bureaucratic caution. It is the only way to know whether a tool is safe for the people in front of you.

A model's performance is anchored to the conditions under which it was trained. Those conditions move:

  • Disease prevalence changes — seasonally, epidemiologically, after a new vaccination programme
  • Equipment is replaced or protocols are updated
  • Referral patterns change, altering the case mix reaching the model
  • Coding or documentation practices change, shifting the meaning of input variables

The defining danger is that degradation is silent. There is no error message. A model quietly becomes less accurate while continuing to produce confident outputs in a familiar format. Only active monitoring detects it — which is why continuous performance surveillance is a clinical-governance obligation rather than an IT task.

Covered in Module 3 as a diagnostic risk; here we consider it as an institutional one.

  • Automation bias. Deferring to the machine against one's own judgement. The UNDP paper explicitly warns that if AI substituted for clinical due diligence, "clinicians might engage in 'automation bias' and not consider whether an AI technology meets their needs or those of the patient."
  • Deskilling. The longer-term concern. If trainees never interpret films unaided because software always offers a preliminary read, the profession's independent capability erodes — and with it, the ability to detect when the software is wrong.
  • Loss of the clinical signal. The uneasy feeling about a patient who "looks unwell" is real information a model cannot access. Systems must preserve a route for it to override an algorithmic reassurance.
  • Accountability diffusion. When a decision emerges partly from an algorithm, responsibility becomes easy to disclaim. No regulator or coroner accepts this.

• Shadow AI. Staff using unapproved public tools with identifiable patient data — in practice the most common and least detected breach in hospitals today.
  • Re-identification. De-identified datasets can often be re-linked, particularly with rare conditions, precise dates or imaging.
  • Cross-border data flows. Patient data leaving the country to an overseas cloud provider, frequently without adequate contractual protection or institutional awareness.
  • Ransomware and system dependency. As clinical workflow becomes dependent on AI systems, their unavailability becomes a patient-safety issue. Every deployment needs a documented downtime procedure.
  • Prompt injection. Hostile instructions concealed in a document an AI assistant processes, causing it to ignore safeguards or disclose information — an emerging and under-appreciated risk for any assistant that reads external content.

Most institutions will buy rather than build. That transfers execution but not accountability.

  • Opacity. Vendors may decline to disclose training data or model behaviour as proprietary, leaving you unable to assess suitability for your population.
  • The pilot graveyard. Donor-funded or vendor-subsidised pilots that end when funding ends, leaving staff trained on a tool they no longer have — and more cynical about the next one.
  • Lock-in and cost escalation. Deep integration makes exit expensive and weakens your negotiating position at renewal.
  • Licensing and access. The UNDP paper raises the concern that in developing-country settings AI use "may be contingent upon restrictive contractual licensing terms that further limit its diffusion and use."
  • Model withdrawal. A vendor may discontinue or materially change a model you have built a clinical pathway around.

A risk specific to our context and easy to overlook. AI could reduce inequity by extending scarce expertise — or entrench it, if benefits accrue only where connectivity, electricity, devices and digital literacy already exist.

The pattern to guard against: an urban tertiary hospital acquires sophisticated AI while rural facilities lack basic diagnostics, and the outcome gap widens. The WEF's vision explicitly includes "leapfrogging by low- or middle-income countries" — but leapfrogging is a possibility, not a promise. It requires deliberate design choices about where tools are deployed and who they are built to serve.

Realistic consequences of an AI-related clinical failure include patient harm and complaint, professional regulatory investigation of the clinician who signed the decision, institutional liability, and — where AI use was not disclosed — a serious breach of trust with patients and the public.

An honest legal reality: liability frameworks for clinical AI remain unsettled in most jurisdictions. In practice this means the clinician and the institution carry the risk while the vendor's exposure is limited by contract. Read the indemnity clauses before deployment, not afterwards.

The governing principle

You may delegate a task to an algorithm. You cannot delegate responsibility for the patient. Before any deployment, test it against one question: if this system contributes to a patient being harmed, can we explain what it did, why we believed it was safe here, what we monitored, and what a clinician was expected to check? If you cannot answer all four, it is not ready.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the pre-mortem
practitioner.text: Before approving any clinical AI deployment, hold a fifteen-minute pre-mortem with clinical, nursing, IT and governance colleagues: "It is one year from now. This system contributed to a serious patient safety incident. What happened?" Teams surface risks in this exercise that no checklist elicits — because it gives permission to voice doubts that formal approval processes discourage. Record the answers and address the top three before going live.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Take one AI tool your institution uses or is considering. Score it 1–5 on each of the eight risk categories in this module. For your three highest scores, write the specific control that would reduce them — who checks what, how often, and what triggers withdrawal of the tool. Bring this to your clinical governance or quality committee. You have produced a defensible first-pass clinical AI risk assessment.

takeaways: In healthcare, AI failure can mean patient harm — false negatives, false positives, alert fatigue and workflow harm are all real mechanisms
Algorithmic bias is invisible without testing, systematic in effect, and self-reinforcing over time
Tools trained on unlike populations may systematically underperform for your patients despite impressive published figures
Dataset shift causes silent degradation — only active monitoring detects it
Automation bias and deskilling erode the profession's ability to detect when the machine is wrong
Shadow AI is the most common real-world confidentiality breach in hospitals
Liability frameworks remain unsettled; in practice clinicians and institutions carry the risk
AI can narrow or widen the digital divide depending on deliberate deployment choices

quiz.q: A screening model's performance declines gradually over two years as local disease prevalence and imaging equipment change. This is:
opts: Dataset shift — silent degradation requiring active monitoring to detect
quiz.fb: Dataset shift produces no error message. Continuous performance monitoring is a clinical governance obligation, not an IT nicety.

quiz.q: Why is algorithmic bias more dangerous than an individual clinician's bias?
opts: It is not — they are equivalent
It is invisible without testing, applied systematically to every patient, and compounds over time
quiz.fb: Scale, invisibility and the self-reinforcing data loop distinguish algorithmic bias from individual bias.

quiz.q: A system generates a very high volume of alerts, most of which are not clinically significant. The principal danger is:
opts: Alert fatigue — clinicians dismiss alerts reflexively, including true ones, potentially reducing safety below baseline
quiz.fb: Over-alerting can make a system net-harmful. Alert burden must be measured and managed as a safety parameter.

quiz.q: 'Deskilling' in the context of clinical AI refers to:
opts: Staff forgetting to use the software
Erosion of independent professional capability, reducing the ability to detect when the AI is wrong
quiz.fb: If trainees never practise unaided interpretation, the profession loses the expertise needed to catch algorithmic errors.

quiz.q: Under current liability frameworks in most jurisdictions, when AI contributes to a clinical error:
opts: The clinician and institution generally carry the risk while vendor exposure is limited by contract
The vendor automatically assumes legal responsibility
quiz.fb: Liability for clinical AI is unsettled, but in practice responsibility rests with the professional and institution. Read indemnity clauses before deployment.

quiz.q: The most common real-world confidentiality breach involving AI in hospitals today is:
opts: Staff entering identifiable patient information into unapproved public AI tools
quiz.fb: Shadow AI is widespread, usually well-intentioned, and best addressed with clear policy plus an accessible approved alternative.

healthcare.title: AI for Health Systems in Nepal & Developing Countries
healthcare.summary: Leapfrogging, workforce shortage and building for constraint
objectives: Quantify the health workforce and access gap that AI is often proposed to address
Understand what 'leapfrogging' realistically means — and what it requires
Apply the WHO-ITU RISE framework for equitable AI adoption
Identify the specific opportunities most relevant to Nepal and comparable systems
Recognise the failure patterns that repeatedly defeat health technology projects in these settings
Understand why locally-owned priorities outperform imported solutions

sections.h: The gap that defines the opportunity
sections.html:
The case for AI in developing-country health systems begins with arithmetic. Citing WHO data, the UNDP background paper reports that:

  • More than 40% of all countries have fewer than 10 medical doctors per 10,000 people.
  • Over 55% have fewer than 40 nursing and midwifery personnel per 10,000 people.
  • Only a third to a half of the global population could obtain essential health services as of 2017.

Looking forward, BCG cites an estimated global shortfall of approximately 10 million health workers by 2030. This shortage cannot be trained away within the timeframe in which the need exists.

That is the honest premise of this module. AI is not attractive here because it is modern. It is attractive because the expertise required does not exist in sufficient quantity and will not for decades — and tools that extend the reach of the expertise that does exist may be the only realistic path to broadened access.

The World Economic Forum explicitly includes "leapfrogging by low- or middle-income countries" among the outcomes AI could enable, noting that in LMICs the focus will be on "establishing foundational technology and expanding access to quality care in order to address ongoing challenges such as high disease burden and weak health information systems."

The mobile-phone analogy is instructive but frequently misused. Nepal did not build a national copper telephone network and then replace it — it moved directly to mobile. The analogous health opportunity is to avoid replicating a decade of fragmented, non-interoperable hospital IT and move directly to shared, standards-based digital infrastructure.

But leapfrogging has preconditions. Mobile telephony leapfrogged because handsets became cheap, networks were commercially viable, and no literacy or institutional change was required to make a call. Clinical AI requires data, connectivity, electricity, trained staff, governance and a referral pathway. Where those are absent, there is nothing to leap from. Leapfrogging is a possibility to be engineered, not a phenomenon to be awaited.

sections.h: The RISE framework — a practical guide for LMIC adoption
sections.html:
The Global Initiative on AI for Health (GI-AI4H) — led by the World Health Organization with the International Telecommunication Union and the World Intellectual Property Organization — proposes the RISE framework as a pragmatic approach for responsible AI across diverse health systems. It is the most directly applicable framework in this programme for a country in Nepal's position.

  • R — Robust Capacity Building. Empower local professionals through training and knowledge sharing: specialised training on AI development, evaluation and ethics for healthcare professionals; open knowledge repositories; mentorship pairing LMIC and global experts; and research partnerships that build in-country expertise.
  • I — Inclusive Research Agenda. Ensure research addresses local priorities. Countries including South Africa and Mozambique stressed localisation over one-size-fits-all approaches, calling for a research agenda driven by LMIC needs and aligned with cultural context and health priorities.
  • S — Smart and Accessible Infrastructure. Build affordable, interoperable systems suited to resource-constrained environments — shared repositories, open standards for quality and benchmarking, and context-appropriate system design.
  • E — Equitable and Secure Data Practices. Fair, safe, transparent data collection so models are accurate for diverse populations — including algorithm audits, bias checks, inclusive data governance committees, and policies enabling model training on under-resourced populations.

The authors stress that these components are modular and mutually reinforcing rather than sequential — countries prioritise and phase them according to existing capacity, regulatory maturity and health system needs. The underlying initiative rests on three pillars: ENABLE (governance standards and technical guidance), FACILITATE (global community and pooled resources) and IMPLEMENT (sustainable country-level models).

Drawing together the evidence from Module 4 and the constraints described above, the applications with the strongest case in Nepal and comparable systems are:

  1. Tuberculosis radiograph triage. High disease burden, radiography already available at district level, and the binding constraint is interpretation capacity rather than equipment.
  2. Diabetic retinopathy screening. Rising diabetes prevalence, severe ophthalmologist scarcity, well-validated technology, and a treatable outcome — provided the treatment pathway exists.
  3. Decision support for frontline and community health workers. Extending safe practice further down the workforce pyramid is arguably the highest-leverage application in a country where community health volunteers are the first and often only point of contact.
  4. Triage and referral support. Where travel to care is costly and difficult, improving the decision about whether and where to travel has direct clinical and economic value.
  5. Nepali-language patient communication. Instructions, consent and health information in the language the patient actually speaks — a genuine equity gain.
  6. Public health surveillance. Operating on data that already exists in routine reporting, with no new devices required at the point of care.
  7. Administrative and operational efficiency. Scheduling, records, supply chain — lower risk, faster measurable return, and it builds the data discipline everything else depends on.

sections.h: Why health technology projects fail here — the recurring patterns
sections.html:
• The pilot that never scales. Donor-funded, externally staffed, ends with the grant. The UNDP paper is clear that adoption "should strengthen local health systems and be owned and driven by the needs and priorities of developing country governments and stakeholders." Ownership is the variable that predicts survival.
  • The imported solution. Built for a different population, disease profile, equipment standard and workflow — and never revalidated locally.
  • Infrastructure assumptions. Reliable electricity, connectivity and device availability assumed rather than verified. A tool requiring continuous cloud connectivity is unusable in facilities where it matters most.
  • The missing pathway. Detection deployed without treatment capacity.
  • The data foundation that was never built. Models proposed on data that does not exist, is not linked, or is not reliable.
  • Workforce readiness overlooked. Tools introduced without the training, time or authority for staff to use them well — or to override them.

The design principle that follows

Prefer tools that degrade gracefully: work offline or with intermittent connectivity, run on modest hardware, tolerate imperfect data, and fail visibly rather than silently. In a well-resourced hospital these are conveniences. In a district facility they determine whether the tool is used at all. Ask every vendor directly: "What happens when the internet is down for six hours?"

The strategic question for any developing country is whether AI adoption builds domestic capability or deepens dependence on external providers. The RISE framework's emphasis on capacity building and in-country expertise is a direct answer.

Practical implications for institutions and individuals:

  • Insist on knowledge transfer in every vendor contract — documented, with named local staff trained and able to maintain the system.
  • Retain your data and the right to use it. A contract permitting a vendor to train on your patients' data while restricting your own access is a bad bargain, however low the licence fee.
  • Invest in local validation capability. The ability to independently evaluate a model on your own population is the single most valuable institutional capability in this field.
  • Support local research and datasets that represent your population — no one else will build them for you.
  • Develop the professionals. This programme is a starting point; sustained capability requires structured, continuing development.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the six-hour question
practitioner.text: When any vendor presents to your institution, ask one question early: "What happens to this system when the internet is down for six hours, or the power fails?" The answer tells you immediately whether the product was designed for a setting like yours or for a well-connected teaching hospital elsewhere. It is also the fastest way to identify which vendors have genuinely worked in comparable environments.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Apply the RISE framework to your own institution. Under each of the four components — Robust capacity building, Inclusive research, Smart infrastructure, Equitable data — write one honest sentence on where you stand today and one specific action that would strengthen it within twelve months. Be candid: this is a self-assessment, not a funding application. The gaps you identify are the real starting point for your AI strategy.

takeaways: Over 40% of countries have fewer than 10 doctors per 10,000 people; a global shortfall of ~10 million health workers is projected by 2030
AI matters here because expertise is scarce and cannot be trained fast enough — not because it is modern
Leapfrogging is possible but has preconditions: data, connectivity, power, skills, governance and pathways
The WHO-ITU-WIPO RISE framework — capacity, inclusive research, smart infrastructure, equitable data — is the most applicable model
Priority applications: TB triage, retinopathy screening, frontline worker decision support, referral triage, Nepali-language communication, surveillance
Projects fail through unowned pilots, imported solutions, infrastructure assumptions and missing pathways
Prefer tools that degrade gracefully; insist on knowledge transfer and data rights to build capability rather than dependency

quiz.q: According to WHO data cited in the UNDP paper, more than 40% of all countries have:
opts: Fewer than 10 medical doctors per 10,000 people
quiz.fb: This workforce scarcity — alongside fewer than 40 nurses/midwives per 10,000 in over 55% of countries — is the core premise for AI in these settings.

quiz.q: The 'S' in the WHO-ITU RISE framework stands for:
quiz.fb: RISE = Robust capacity building, Inclusive research agenda, Smart and accessible infrastructure, Equitable and secure data practices.

quiz.q: Countries such as South Africa and Mozambique emphasised which principle in WHO-ITU consultations?
opts: Localisation over one-size-fits-all approaches, driven by local needs and context
quiz.fb: An inclusive research agenda driven by LMIC priorities and aligned with local cultural and health contexts was a consistent theme.

quiz.q: Which design property matters most for a tool intended for district-level facilities?
opts: Graceful degradation — working offline, on modest hardware, failing visibly
quiz.fb: In well-resourced hospitals these are conveniences; in district facilities they determine whether the tool can be used at all.

quiz.q: The UNDP paper argues that AI adoption in developing countries should be:
opts: Owned and driven by the needs and priorities of local governments and stakeholders
quiz.fb: Local ownership is the variable that most reliably predicts whether a health technology project survives beyond its pilot funding.

quiz.q: A vendor contract allows the supplier to train models on your patients' data but restricts your own access to it. This is:
opts: A bad bargain that builds dependency rather than local capability
quiz.fb: Retaining data rights and insisting on knowledge transfer are how institutions build capability instead of deepening dependence.

healthcare.title: Ethics, Governance & Regulation
healthcare.summary: Consent, oversight, regulatory frameworks and clinical governance
objectives: Apply core ethical principles to AI in clinical care
Understand how AI-enabled medical devices are regulated internationally and what that implies locally
Understand WHO guidance and the global governance landscape
Build a clinical AI governance structure with clear accountability
Handle consent, transparency and disclosure to patients
Design validation, monitoring and incident procedures for deployed AI

sections.html:
Clinical AI raises no genuinely new ethical principles. It applies familiar ones under unfamiliar conditions:

  • Beneficence and non-maleficence. Does this tool improve outcomes, and what harms does it introduce? Both must be measured, not assumed.
  • Autonomy. Does the patient understand that AI is involved, and can they decline?
  • Justice. Does it narrow or widen inequity? Who benefits, and who is left out?
  • Confidentiality. Health information carries the strongest duty of protection in professional practice.
  • Accountability. A named professional remains answerable for every clinical decision.

The WHO has articulated ethical principles for AI in health emphasising protecting autonomy, promoting human well-being and safety, ensuring transparency and explainability, fostering responsibility and accountability, ensuring inclusiveness and equity, and promoting responsive and sustainable AI. These map directly onto the principles above.

sections.h: How AI in medicine is regulated
sections.html:
Most clinical AI falls under medical device regulation as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). Key international reference points:

  • Risk-based classification. Regulatory burden scales with potential harm. A tool that informs a clinician is treated differently from one that drives treatment directly.
  • EU AI Act. Establishes a risk-tiered approach, with many healthcare applications falling into higher-risk categories carrying heightened obligations.
  • US FDA. Clears AI-enabled devices, predominantly in imaging — the WEF notes more than 70% of approvals are imaging-related.
  • Post-market surveillance. Increasingly central, because models change and populations drift. The WEF calls for moving "from waiting for guidelines to proactively building trust" through improved post-market surveillance and AI ethics committees.

The npj Health Systems paper notes the diversity of approaches globally — from HIPAA in the United States to Saudi Arabia's PDPL, India's DPDP Act, Zambia's National AI Strategy and Malawi's Data Protection Act — concluding that what is needed are "globally coordinated yet locally adaptable governance frameworks."

The Nepal position — verify before you rely

Nepal's framework for AI-enabled medical software continues to develop, alongside the Privacy Act (2075), national digital health initiatives, and the oversight roles of the Department of Drug Administration and the Nepal Health Research Council for research involving human subjects and health data. Regulatory expectations in this area are evolving quickly. Always confirm current requirements with your institution's ethics committee, the relevant national authority, and qualified legal advice before deploying any clinical AI or sharing patient data. This programme teaches the framework and reasoning; it does not substitute for the current regulatory instrument.

sections.h: The regulatory gap in developing countries
sections.html:
The UNDP paper observes that regulation of AI in healthcare "is still in its infancy," with many countries issuing plans, guidelines or codes highlighting ethical principles "without passing much substantive law." The npj paper similarly warns that rapid adoption "can heighten risks and widen existing inequalities due to the lack of standardized governance and the regulatory lag in many countries."

This creates a practical dilemma. Waiting for complete regulation means forgoing benefit; proceeding without it means bearing risk. The workable middle path is institutional governance that anticipates regulation — adopting recognised international standards voluntarily, documenting decisions as though they will be scrutinised, and building the evidence a future regulator would require. Institutions that do this are not slowed down; they are the ones able to move when rules arrive.

• Board or executive. Approves AI strategy and risk appetite; receives regular reporting on deployed systems, performance and incidents; retains ultimate accountability.
  • Clinical AI committee. Multidisciplinary — clinicians, nursing, pharmacy, IT, information governance, ethics, quality and patient representation. Approves clinical deployments and reviews performance.
  • Clinical owner. A named senior clinician accountable for each deployed tool: appropriate use, monitoring, and patient outcomes.
  • Independent validation. Assessment by people who did not procure or build the system. Independence is the point.
  • Information governance. Data flows, consent, contracts, cross-border transfer.
  • An AI register. A single inventory of every AI system in clinical or administrative use — including features embedded in software you already own. Institutions consistently discover more than expected, and this is the practical first governance artefact.

Three distinct questions, often conflated:

  1. Consent to care involving AI. Where AI materially influences a clinical decision, patients should be able to know and to decline. Practice varies for background tools, but the direction of travel is toward disclosure.
  2. Consent for data use. Using patient data to develop or improve models is a separate purpose requiring its own basis — clinical consent does not cover it.
  3. Transparency about AI-generated communication. If material given to a patient was AI-drafted, honesty is the safe position.

A practical standard: would this patient be surprised, or feel deceived, if they later learned how AI was used in their care? If yes, disclose in advance. Trust, once lost across a community, is extraordinarily expensive to rebuild — and in health systems that depend on community confidence, that cost is measured in people who stop attending.

1. Pre-deployment validation. Assess performance on your population before go-live wherever feasible. Where a full local study is impossible, run a silent period — the model runs without influencing decisions while its outputs are compared against clinical outcomes.
  2. Define the operating threshold clinically. Sensitivity–specificity trade-offs must be set by clinicians who understand the consequences of each error, not accepted as vendor defaults.
  3. Monitor continuously. Performance, alert volume, override rates, subgroup performance and complaints — with pre-agreed escalation triggers.
  4. Report incidents. AI-related safety events must enter the same incident system as any other clinical incident, and be reviewable.
  5. Define withdrawal criteria in advance. Agree before deployment what performance would cause you to switch the system off — and who has authority to do it, without needing a committee meeting.

sections.h: Research, publication and the evidence base
sections.html:
If your institution evaluates a tool, that evaluation is research and requires ethics approval. Two obligations follow.

First, use recognised reporting standards — CONSORT-AI, SPIRIT-AI and STARD-AI exist precisely to make AI studies comparable and honest.

Second, and importantly for global equity: publish, including negative results. The evidence base for clinical AI in South Asian and African populations is thin, and it is thin partly because evaluations conducted in these settings are rarely written up. A well-conducted local validation showing that a tool does not transfer is a genuine contribution to global knowledge — and protects other institutions from repeating an expensive mistake.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: start the register today
practitioner.text: Before writing any AI strategy, compile a list of every system in your institution using AI or machine learning — including features already embedded in software you licence, such as imaging post-processing, transcription or triage modules. This takes a fortnight and consistently reveals tools operating in clinical use that were never assessed, approved or monitored. That register is the single most valuable governance document a hospital produces in its first year of AI oversight.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Draft a one-page clinical AI governance note for your institution covering: who approves clinical AI deployments; who the named clinical owner would be; what pre-deployment validation you would require; what you would monitor monthly; what triggers withdrawal and who can authorise it; and how AI involvement would be disclosed to patients. If your institution has none of this, your note is the first draft of its policy.

takeaways: Clinical AI raises familiar ethical principles under unfamiliar conditions — beneficence, autonomy, justice, confidentiality, accountability
Most clinical AI is regulated as Software as a Medical Device on a risk-based basis; post-market surveillance is increasingly central
Regulation lags in many countries — institutional governance that anticipates regulation is the workable path
An AI register is the practical first governance artefact and usually reveals unassessed systems
Consent to care involving AI and consent for data use are separate; disclose if a patient would feel deceived to learn later
Validate locally or run a silent period; set thresholds clinically; monitor subgroups; define withdrawal criteria in advance
Publish local evaluations including negative results — the evidence base for our populations depends on it

quiz.q: Most clinical AI tools are regulated internationally as:
opts: Software as a Medical Device, on a risk-based classification
quiz.fb: SaMD frameworks scale regulatory requirements to potential harm, and increasingly emphasise post-market surveillance.

quiz.q: Your institution wants to deploy a model but cannot conduct a full local validation study. The best alternative is:
opts: Rely solely on the vendor's published figures
Run a silent period where the model operates without influencing decisions while outputs are compared to outcomes
quiz.fb: A silent period generates local performance evidence without exposing patients to an unvalidated tool.

quiz.q: Consent for clinical care involving AI and consent for using patient data to train models are:
opts: Separate purposes each requiring their own basis
quiz.fb: Clinical consent does not extend to model development. Data use for AI is a distinct purpose requiring its own lawful basis.

quiz.q: Why does the npj Health Systems paper argue governance frameworks must be 'globally coordinated yet locally adaptable'?
opts: Because approaches differ across jurisdictions while risks are shared, and local health system contexts vary
quiz.fb: Frameworks such as HIPAA, PDPL, India's DPDP Act and others reflect different legal traditions, but the underlying risks require coordination.

quiz.q: Publishing a local validation showing a tool does NOT transfer to your population is:
opts: Only worthwhile if results are positive
A genuine contribution that strengthens the evidence base and protects other institutions
quiz.fb: Negative results are scarce and valuable — especially for South Asian and African populations where the evidence base is thin.

quiz.q: Withdrawal criteria for a deployed clinical AI tool should be:
opts: Agreed in advance, with named authority to act without waiting for a committee
quiz.fb: Deciding in advance what performance would cause you to switch a system off — and who can do it immediately — is basic clinical safety governance.

healthcare.title: Implementation: From Pilot to Practice
healthcare.summary: Making it work, making it last, and building your proposal
objectives: Understand why most healthcare AI initiatives fail to scale beyond pilot
Apply the 10-20-70 rule and prioritise change management appropriately
Build a credible business case with a measured baseline and full lifetime cost
Conduct meaningful vendor due diligence for clinical software
Design a pilot with defined success criteria and a stopping rule
Lead clinical colleagues through adoption
Complete a defensible AI use-case proposal for your own institution

sections.html:
BCG's analysis of generative AI in healthcare finds that only around 24% of companies across industries have extracted meaningful value, with healthcare providers at roughly 29% and medtech far behind at 10%. The reasons given are consistent: fragmented initiatives that never reach core processes, no clear link between activity and measurable impact, and low user adoption.

Their prescription is equally consistent. Leading organisations dedicate over 80% of AI investment to reshaping core functions rather than running scattered experiments; they tie AI explicitly to measurable outcomes; and they invest in structured change management, which BCG reports can raise adoption rates from 30% to 60%.

BCG's guidance for healthcare AI in 2026 states the rule plainly: successful innovators dedicate 10% of effort to algorithms, 20% to technology and data, and 70% to people and processes.

This should reorder how you plan. If your implementation plan is mostly about the model and the integration, with training and workflow redesign as a final line item, it is inverted — and it will likely join the 70% of healthcare AI projects that never reach sustained use.

In clinical settings the "70%" means specific things: redesigning the workflow so the tool sits where the decision is made; training staff not only to use it but to challenge it; agreeing who acts on outputs; protecting time for the change; and identifying credible clinical champions. None of this is technology work, and all of it determines success.

sections.h: Building a business case that survives scrutiny
sections.html:
Six elements, and clinical proposals commonly omit two of them:

  1. The problem in operational terms. "Chest radiographs wait an average of nine days for reporting, and 12% of TB diagnoses are delayed beyond four weeks."
  2. The measured baseline. Current performance, quantified before anything changes. This is the element most often skipped, and its absence makes success unprovable.
  3. The intervention. Precisely what the system does, in which mode (assistive, triage, autonomous), and where the human decision sits.
  4. The expected benefit. Conservative, ranged, and expressed in clinical terms — time to treatment, cases detected, avoided travel — not only cost.
  5. The full lifetime cost. Licence, integration, hardware, connectivity, training, validation, monitoring, and clinician time. Licence fees are usually a minority of the total.
  6. Risk and governance. Drawn from Modules 6 and 8, with named owner, monitoring plan and withdrawal criteria.

The efficiency trap

Be careful with business cases built on saving clinician minutes. Ten minutes saved per clinician per day is real for the individual, but it does not become an institutional saving unless the freed time is deliberately redirected to a defined activity — more patients seen, a clinic reopened, backlog cleared. State explicitly what the saved time will be used for, or the benefit will never materialise on paper.

sections.h: Vendor due diligence for clinical software
sections.html:
Ask these before signing:

  • What population was the model trained on — geography, demographics, equipment, disease prevalence?
  • What external, prospective validation exists, and can we see the failure cases?
  • What performance do you commit to in a population like ours, and what happens if it is not met?
  • Can we conduct our own independent validation before and after deployment?
  • Where is patient data processed and stored, and does it leave the country?
  • Will our patients' data be used to train models for other customers?
  • What monitoring, drift detection and alerting are included?
  • What happens when connectivity or power fails?
  • What are the exit terms — can we retrieve our data in a usable form?
  • What indemnity applies if the model contributes to patient harm?
  • What knowledge transfer and local training are included?

A vendor unwilling to answer the validation, data-rights and indemnity questions in writing is not suitable for clinical deployment, whatever the demonstration showed.

sections.h: Designing a pilot that gives you a real answer
sections.html:
1. Narrow scope. One department, one pathway, one measurable outcome.
  2. Measure the baseline first — for at least four weeks before anything changes.
  3. Define success and failure numerically in advance, including the threshold at which you stop.
  4. Run silently or in parallel first where patient safety permits.
  5. Set an end date. Pilots without one become permanent unevaluated systems.
  6. Include the people who will use it in design — clinicians and nurses know the edge cases the vendor does not.
  7. Decide honestly. Scale, redesign, or stop. A well-run pilot concluding "no" has prevented a costly, potentially unsafe mistake.

• Address the job question directly. Clinical staff will wonder whether this replaces them. BCG's outlook frames the realistic answer: AI agents should augment the workforce, with organisations upskilling current workers and redesigning roles. Say this plainly and early — silence breeds resistance.
  • Recruit credible clinical champions. Adoption follows respected clinicians, not administrators or vendors.
  • Train the challenge, not just the click. Staff must be able to recognise when output is wrong and be genuinely empowered to override it — the direct antidote to automation bias.
  • Protect time for learning. Change introduced without protected time is change that does not happen.
  • Embed AI literacy in professional development, as BCG recommends — this is a durable capability, not a one-off training event.
  • Close the loop. Show staff what changed as a result of their use of the tool. Nothing sustains adoption like visible patient benefit.

sections.h: Where to begin — a realistic first year
sections.html:
1. Compile the AI register (Module 8) — two weeks, high value.
  2. Issue an acceptable-use policy for generative AI tools, addressing shadow AI immediately at no cost.
  3. Name accountability — an executive owner and a multidisciplinary clinical AI committee.
  4. Assess against RISE (Module 7) and identify your weakest component.
  5. Choose one low-risk operational project with a measured baseline and a stopping rule.
  6. Build validation capability — the ability to evaluate a model on your own population is your most valuable long-term asset.
  7. Develop your people. This programme is a start; sustained competence requires structured continuing development.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: measure before you build
practitioner.text: The most common reason a promising clinical AI project cannot be scaled is that nobody recorded what performance looked like beforehand. Before writing a specification or meeting a vendor, spend four weeks measuring the current pathway — time to report, time to treatment, volumes, error rates. That baseline is the cheapest work in the entire programme and the only thing that converts an impression into evidence.

activity.title: Capstone: your AI use-case proposal
activity.text: Complete the proposal you began in Module 4 by adding: the deployment mode (assistive, triage or autonomous) and where the human decision sits; the local validation or silent-period plan; the fairness and subgroup checks you would run; the monitoring plan with escalation triggers; the full lifetime cost including training and monitoring; the named clinical owner; and the pilot's numeric success criteria, end date and withdrawal threshold. The finished document is a genuine, defensible proposal for your institution — and the practical outcome of this programme.

takeaways: Only about a quarter of organisations extract meaningful value from GenAI; healthcare providers sit near that benchmark
Apply 10-20-70 — most of the effort is people and process, not algorithms
Structured change management can lift adoption from roughly 30% to 60%
Business cases need a measured baseline and full lifetime cost; state explicitly how saved time will be used
Demand written answers on validation, data rights and indemnity before signing
Pilots need numeric success criteria, an end date and a stopping rule agreed in advance
Address job fears directly, recruit clinical champions, and train staff to challenge the tool
Local validation capability is the most valuable long-term institutional asset

quiz.q: The 10-20-70 rule for successful AI implementation allocates effort as:
opts: 10% algorithms, 20% technology and data, 70% people and processes
quiz.fb: The overwhelming majority of effort belongs to people and process. Plans weighted toward the model are inverted and usually fail to sustain.

quiz.q: BCG reports that structured change management can raise user adoption rates:
quiz.fb: Low adoption is a leading reason healthcare AI fails to scale, and structured change management roughly doubles it.

quiz.q: A business case built on saving each clinician ten minutes per day will only deliver institutional benefit if:
opts: The freed time is deliberately redirected to a defined activity such as clearing backlog
quiz.fb: Time saved that is not explicitly redirected never appears as institutional benefit — state the intended use in the proposal.

quiz.q: Which vendor answer should be treated as disqualifying for clinical deployment?
opts: Refusing to answer validation, data-rights and indemnity questions in writing
quiz.fb: Written commitments on validation evidence, data rights and indemnity are minimum requirements for software influencing patient care.

quiz.q: A pilot without a pre-agreed end date and stopping rule typically:
quiz.fb: Undefined pilots quietly become production systems that nobody ever formally assessed or approved.

quiz.q: The most valuable long-term institutional capability in clinical AI is:
opts: The ability to independently validate a model on your own population
quiz.fb: Independent local validation capability is what lets you judge any tool, from any vendor, for your own patients — permanently.

finance.title: AI Foundations for Banking
finance.summary: The concepts and vocabulary every banker now needs
objectives: Distinguish artificial intelligence, machine learning, deep learning and generative AI — and know which matters where in a bank
Explain supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning using banking examples
Understand how a machine-learning model differs from the statistical scorecards banks have used for decades
Read and interpret the core performance metrics used to judge financial models: accuracy, precision, recall, AUC and the Gini coefficient
Speak credibly with vendors, IT teams and regulators using correct terminology

sections.h: Why this matters now, and to you
sections.html:
Artificial intelligence has moved from a technology conversation to a governance conversation. Nepal Rastra Bank has issued Artificial Intelligence Guidelines covering licensed institutions — Class A through D, along with payment system operators and payment service providers — and those guidelines place ultimate accountability for AI outcomes on the board and senior management, not on the IT department.

That single fact changes who needs to understand this material. A credit officer approving a model-assisted decision, a compliance officer signing off on transaction monitoring, a branch manager explaining a declined loan to a customer — each is now operating inside an AI-governed process. This module builds the vocabulary and the mental models that make the rest of the programme possible.

Industry evidence · SAS / Juniper

This is not a distant trend. Juniper Research projects that AI spending in the banking industry will reach US$85 billion by 2030, implying a compound annual growth rate of around 55%. SAS research finds that 60% of banking organisations have already deployed generative AI use cases, with a further 38% expecting to do so within two years.

“Trust is earned in drops and lost in buckets.”
— SAS, From Algorithms to Impact: Banking's AI Future

These words are used loosely in vendor presentations. Precision protects you.

  • Artificial Intelligence (AI) — the broad field of systems performing tasks that normally require human intelligence. A rules-based fraud engine is AI, even without learning.
  • Machine Learning (ML) — systems that learn patterns from historical data rather than following rules a person wrote. This is what powers modern credit scoring and fraud detection.
  • Deep Learning — ML using multi-layered neural networks. Strong on unstructured data: images, documents, voice, natural language.
  • Generative AI — models that produce new content: text, summaries, code, images. This is the large-language-model wave now entering banking operations (Module 5).

A practical translation: most decisioning in banks (credit, fraud, pricing) is machine learning. Most productivity use (drafting, summarising, searching policy) is generative AI. They carry different risks and different regulatory expectations.

Industry evidence · FIS

FIS draws the same three-way distinction in AI Alchemy: machine learning develops algorithms that find patterns in data; predictive AI forecasts future outcomes and underpins process automation; and generative AI creates new content from prompts using large language models. Machine learning is the broader concept that contains both of the others — precision in these terms is what allows you to ask a vendor the right question.

sections.h: Three ways a model learns — with banking examples
sections.html:
• Supervised learning — learns from labelled historical outcomes. You show it thousands of past loans marked "defaulted" or "repaid", and it learns to estimate default probability on new applications. Nearly all credit and fraud models are supervised.
  • Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels. Used to segment customers into behavioural groups, or to flag transactions that simply do not resemble anything normal — valuable in AML where you do not know every fraud pattern in advance.
  • Reinforcement learning — learns by trial, error and reward. Used in areas like collections strategy optimisation, dynamic pricing and algorithmic execution. Rare in Nepali banks today, but relevant as sophistication grows.

sections.h: How this differs from the scorecard you already know
sections.html:
Banks have used statistical models for decades. A traditional credit scorecard is typically a logistic regression: a modest number of variables, each with a transparent weight, producing points that sum to a score. Its great virtue is that it is interpretable — you can tell an applicant exactly which factors counted against them.

A modern machine-learning model may consider hundreds of variables and capture non-linear interactions a scorecard cannot. It typically predicts better. Its weakness is opacity: the reasoning is distributed across the model rather than readable from a table.

This is the central trade-off of AI in regulated finance, and you will meet it repeatedly in this programme: predictive power versus explainability. NRB's guidelines require AI applications to be transparent, explainable, fair and accountable — which means the more powerful model is not automatically the permissible one.

Deeper dive: why "the model is more accurate" is an incomplete argument

A vendor demonstrating a two-point Gini improvement is describing a benefit. The relevant questions are: can we explain individual decisions to customers and supervisors; can we evidence that it does not discriminate; can we monitor it for drift; and who is accountable when it errs. A model that cannot satisfy those is a liability regardless of its accuracy.

sections.h: Reading model performance like a banker
sections.html:
You do not need to build models, but you must be able to challenge the numbers put in front of you.

  • Accuracy — share of all predictions that were correct. Dangerously misleading for rare events: if 0.5% of transactions are fraudulent, a model that approves everything is 99.5% "accurate" and catches nothing.
  • Precision — of the cases the model flagged, how many were genuine. Low precision means your investigation team drowns in false positives.
  • Recall (sensitivity) — of all genuine cases, how many the model caught. Low recall means real fraud or real defaults slipping through.
  • AUC / ROC — a single measure (0.5 = random, 1.0 = perfect) of how well the model separates good from bad across all thresholds.
  • Gini coefficient — the credit industry's preferred cousin of AUC (Gini = 2 × AUC − 1). A retail scorecard with a Gini around 0.4–0.6 is typically considered workable, though this varies by portfolio and market.

Precision and recall pull against each other. Tightening a fraud model to catch more crime inevitably inconveniences more honest customers. That balance is a business decision, not a technical one — and it belongs to you, not to the data scientist.

Structured data sits in neat rows and columns: account balances, transaction amounts, repayment histories, demographics. It is what core banking systems produce and what traditional models consume.

Unstructured data is everything else: scanned loan files, letters of credit, KYC documents, call recordings, emails, customer complaints. Industry estimates commonly put the majority of institutional data in this category, and until recently banks could not use it at scale. Deep learning and generative AI change that — which is precisely why document-heavy Nepali banking processes are such fertile ground for automation.

Three corrections worth carrying into every vendor meeting:

  • It is not reasoning like a human. It is high-dimensional pattern recognition. It has no understanding of your credit policy unless that policy is represented in its data or instructions.
  • It is not objective. A model trained on your historical decisions inherits your historical preferences, including the ones you would not defend publicly.
  • It is not self-maintaining. Economies shift, customer behaviour shifts, fraud typologies shift. A model left unmonitored degrades — a phenomenon called drift, covered in Module 8.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the question that reframes a vendor pitch
practitioner.text: When a vendor presents an AI solution, ask: "What data was this model trained on, and how similar is that population to our customers?" A fraud model trained on urban card transactions in another market may perform poorly on remittance-driven, mobile-first Nepali customers. Model performance is not portable — it is a property of the data it learned from.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Identify one decision in your own department that currently relies on judgement or a simple rule — a limit approval, a flag for review, a customer segmentation. Write down: (a) what outcome you would want a model to predict, (b) what historical data would be needed to train it, and (c) whether a wrong prediction would be more costly as a false positive or a false negative. You have just written the opening of a model specification.

takeaways: AI is the field, ML learns from data, deep learning handles unstructured data, generative AI creates content — each carries different risk
Supervised learning dominates credit and fraud; unsupervised learning finds unknown patterns in AML
Machine learning usually predicts better than scorecards but is harder to explain — and NRB requires explainability
Accuracy is misleading for rare events; precision, recall, AUC and Gini are the meaningful measures
The precision–recall trade-off is a business decision owned by the business, not by the data team

quiz.q: A fraud model reports 99.4% accuracy on a portfolio where 0.6% of transactions are fraudulent. What should your first reaction be?
opts: Accuracy is misleading here; ask for precision and recall
Accuracy is the only metric that matters
Ask them to raise accuracy to 100%
quiz.fb: With rare events, a model that flags nothing still scores ~99.4%. Precision and recall reveal whether it actually catches fraud.

quiz.q: Which learning type is best suited to detecting entirely new, previously unseen money-laundering patterns?
opts: Supervised learning on labelled past cases
Unsupervised learning that flags abnormal behaviour
quiz.fb: Unsupervised methods find what does not fit normal patterns — valuable when you cannot label typologies you have never seen.

quiz.q: The central trade-off when replacing a logistic-regression scorecard with a complex ML model is…
quiz.fb: ML often predicts better but is harder to explain — and NRB's guidelines require transparency, explainability, fairness and accountability.

quiz.q: Under NRB's AI Guidelines, ultimate accountability for outcomes produced by a bank's AI systems rests with…
opts: The board of directors and senior management
quiz.fb: Accountability sits with the board and senior management — which is why business leaders, not just technologists, must understand these systems.

quiz.q: 'Recall' in a credit or fraud model measures…
opts: What proportion of genuine cases the model successfully caught
How many flagged cases were genuine
quiz.fb: Recall = of all true cases, how many were caught. Precision = of those flagged, how many were true. Low recall means real losses slipping through.

finance.title: The Data Foundation: Why Most Bank AI Projects Fail
finance.summary: Data readiness, quality and the traps that sink models
objectives: Explain why data quality — not algorithm choice — determines the success of most banking AI projects
Identify the principal data problems in Nepali banking: silos, legacy core systems, paper records and inconsistent KYC
Understand training, validation and test splits, and why they protect the bank
Recognise the two most damaging technical traps: data leakage and class imbalance
Assess whether a proposed use case is realistically supported by the data your institution actually holds

sections.html:
A large share of enterprise AI initiatives fail to reach production or deliver their expected value — a pattern consistently reported across industry studies. In banking, the cause is rarely the algorithm. It is almost always the data: fragmented, inconsistent, undocumented, or simply insufficient for the question being asked.

Practitioners routinely describe spending the majority of a project's effort on locating, cleaning and reconciling data rather than modelling it. Any vendor or internal team that glosses over data readiness is describing a demonstration, not a deployment.

Industry evidence · EY & IIF

Research by Ernst & Young and the Institute of International Finance identifies data quality as the single most fundamental bottleneck for financial institutions advancing AI, cited by the vast majority of firms. Data availability and the adaptability of training data rank second.

Almost all institutions surveyed pointed to “noisy, outdated, inaccurate and poorly adaptable unstructured data” as the primary barrier to deployment, with the shortage of labelled data a major constraint on technical implementation. Organisational factors — weak internal stakeholder support and immature technical infrastructure — follow closely behind.

sections.h: Where banking data actually lives — and why that hurts
sections.html:
A typical bank's information is scattered across systems that were never designed to speak to one another:

  • The core banking system holds accounts, balances and transactions.
  • The loan origination system holds application data — often separately from performance data.
  • Card and digital channels hold their own transaction streams.
  • KYC and customer files may be part-digital, part-scanned, part-physical.
  • Branch knowledge — the informal assessment of a borrower — is frequently unrecorded entirely.

To build a credit model you must join application data to subsequent repayment behaviour for the same customer across several of these systems. If customer identification is inconsistent — a national ID recorded differently in two systems, or a customer holding relationships under slightly different names — that join fails silently, and the resulting dataset is quietly wrong.

sections.h: The Nepali context: specific, solvable constraints
sections.html:
Institutions in Nepal face a recognisable set of conditions:

  • Legacy core systems with limited data-extraction capability and short retention of historical states.
  • Paper and scanned records, particularly in older loan files and rural branches — a genuine opportunity for document AI (Module 5), but a barrier for structured modelling today.
  • Thin credit histories. Many customers, especially MSMEs and the newly banked, have limited formal borrowing records, which weakens traditional scoring and makes alternative data attractive — with the fairness cautions covered in Module 3.
  • Rapidly growing digital transaction data from mobile wallets and QR payments, which is often the richest and most under-used asset a bank holds.
  • Language and script inconsistency — Nepali and English, Devanagari and Roman transliteration in names and addresses, which complicates matching and screening.

sections.h: How a model is actually trained: the three-way split
sections.html:
Data is divided before modelling begins:

  1. Training set — the majority of the data; the model learns its parameters here.
  2. Validation set — used to tune settings and compare candidate models.
  3. Test set — held back, untouched, and used once to estimate real-world performance.

In credit, an out-of-time test is stronger still: train on earlier years, test on a later year the model has never seen. This is the only honest way to know whether a model will hold up as conditions change.

Deeper dive: overfitting, in one sentence

A model that memorises the peculiarities of its training data rather than learning generalisable patterns is overfitted — it looks superb in development and disappoints in production. The gap between training performance and hold-out test performance is your early warning, and it is a fair question to put to any model developer or vendor.

Data leakage occurs when information that would not be available at the moment of decision leaks into the training data. It produces spectacular, entirely fictitious performance.

A classic banking example: including a "days past due" field, or the existence of a collections note, when predicting default at application. Both are consequences of default, not predictors available at underwriting. The model appears to achieve extraordinary accuracy, is deployed, and immediately fails — because at the moment a real application arrives, those fields are empty.

The test to apply: for every variable, ask "would we genuinely possess this value, in this form, at the exact moment the decision is made?" If not, it must be removed.

Fraud is rare. Default, in a healthy portfolio, is uncommon. When one outcome represents a very small share of cases, a model can achieve excellent headline accuracy by simply predicting "no" every time.

Practitioners address this with resampling techniques, class weighting, and — critically — by evaluating on precision, recall and related measures rather than accuracy. As a business reviewer, your role is to insist on the right metric and to specify the cost asymmetry: what does a missed fraud cost the bank, versus a false alarm inflicted on a good customer?

NRB's guidelines require compliance with privacy law, including Nepal's Privacy Act (2075), explicit customer consent for the use of personal data, and a customer right to opt out of AI-driven services. That has direct data implications:

  • Lineage — you must be able to trace where each data element came from.
  • Purpose limitation — data gathered for account opening cannot be silently repurposed for unrelated profiling.
  • Consent records — must be maintained and auditable.
  • Retention and access control — training datasets containing customer information are themselves a security asset requiring protection.

Institutions should always work from the current version of NRB's guidelines and circulars, as regulatory expectations in this area continue to evolve.

Industry evidence · BCG

One important nuance from BCG's Generative AI in Banking: classic predictive AI and generative AI run on largely separate technology stacks. Predictive models depend on a mature data warehouse, feature stores and model training pipelines. Generative AI depends instead on pre-trained foundation models, vector stores, caches and retrieval components — and requires no additional model training.

The practical implication for an institution with imperfect data: a weak data warehouse is a genuine blocker for a new credit scorecard, but it is not necessarily a blocker for a document-processing or policy-assistant use case. Data remediation and generative AI pilots can proceed in parallel.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the six-month rule
practitioner.text: Before approving any AI initiative, ask a single grounding question: "Can we assemble a clean, joined dataset for this use case within six months, and do we have at least two to three years of relevant outcome history?" If the honest answer is no, the correct first project is data remediation — not AI. Institutions that skip this step typically spend far more discovering it later.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Pick one use case from your department. List every data field the model would need. Beside each, mark: (A) available and reliable today, (B) exists but is unclean or in another system, (C) not captured at all. If more than a third of your fields fall into B or C, you have just built the business case for a data project — which is a more valuable finding than a failed model.

takeaways: Most banking AI failures are data failures, not algorithm failures
Fragmented core, origination, channel and KYC systems make joining data the hardest step
Train / validation / test splits — ideally out-of-time — are what prove a model will generalise
Data leakage produces fake accuracy; ask whether each field truly exists at the moment of decision
Rare outcomes demand precision and recall, plus an explicit view of the cost of each error type
Consent, lineage, purpose limitation and retention are regulatory requirements, not IT housekeeping

quiz.q: A default-prediction model includes 'number of collection calls made' as a variable and shows remarkable accuracy. What is wrong?
opts: Nothing — it is a strong predictor
Data leakage: that information does not exist at the moment of underwriting
Collection calls should be counted monthly
The variable should be weighted higher
quiz.fb: Collection calls are a consequence of default, unavailable at application. This is textbook leakage — impressive in testing, useless in production.

quiz.q: Why is an out-of-time test set particularly valuable in credit modelling?
opts: It shows whether the model holds up on a later period it never saw
It is required for all marketing models
quiz.fb: Training on earlier periods and testing on a later one is the honest test of whether performance survives changing conditions.

quiz.q: Which is the most realistic first project for a bank whose customer identifiers are inconsistent across core, cards and origination systems?
opts: Deploy a deep-learning credit model immediately
Remediate and reconcile the data foundation
quiz.fb: Models built on a broken join are quietly wrong. Data remediation is unglamorous but is the genuine prerequisite.

quiz.q: NRB's guidelines require, among other things, that banks…
opts: Obtain explicit customer consent for personal-data use and allow opt-out of AI-driven services
Avoid AI in customer service entirely
quiz.fb: Explicit consent, privacy compliance aligned with the Privacy Act, and a customer right to opt out are core requirements.

quiz.q: In a portfolio where 0.3% of transactions are fraudulent, the biggest modelling danger is…
opts: The model will be too slow
Class imbalance — high accuracy achieved by predicting 'not fraud' every time
quiz.fb: Severe class imbalance makes accuracy meaningless; evaluation must use precision, recall and the business cost of each error.

finance.title: AI in Credit Risk & Lending
finance.summary: Scoring, alternative data, early warning and fair lending
objectives: Map where AI is applied across the full credit lifecycle, from origination to collections
