quiz.fb: With 63% of firms building on external foundation models, provider change management becomes part of your own model risk framework.

finance-advanced.title: Explainable AI in Depth
finance-advanced.summary: Why XAI fails in practice, and how to make it work
objectives: Understand the accuracy–interpretability trade-off and when it is real versus assumed
Distinguish interpretable models from post-hoc explanation, and know when each is appropriate
Apply SHAP, LIME and counterfactual explanations, and understand their limitations
Recognise the 'explaining the explanation' problem
Design stakeholder-specific explanations for customers, front-line staff, validators and supervisors
Understand why XAI implementation fails for organisational rather than technical reasons

sections.html:
A 2026 systematic literature review in Applied Artificial Intelligence — Explainable Artificial Intelligence in the Banking Sector by Tuge and Msweli — synthesises 78 peer-reviewed studies and industry reports from 2021 to 2025 using PRISMA 2020 methodology. Its central finding is uncomfortable and important:

There is a persistent gap between XAI's technical promise and its operational deployment in banking. The literature extensively documents XAI's potential to enhance transparency, regulatory compliance and trust. Yet the review finds that technical challenges are "compounded by more fundamental organisational and cultural barriers" — resistance to change, misalignment between technical teams and business units, and the absence of standardised evaluation frameworks.

Their conclusion should shape how your institution approaches this: XAI must evolve from a technical add-on to an embedded organisational capability, requiring structural change in how banks approach AI governance, stakeholder communication and ethical oversight.

The conventional claim is that more accurate models are less interpretable. The review identifies this trade-off as a genuine technical challenge — but practitioners should hold it more sceptically than the phrase suggests.

  • The trade-off is often smaller than assumed. On well-structured tabular credit data, a carefully built logistic regression frequently performs within a few Gini points of a gradient-boosted model. The marginal gain may not survive the explainability cost.
  • It is largest where data is unstructured — documents, images, voice, free text. Here deep models genuinely dominate and interpretable alternatives do not exist.
  • Constrained interpretable models — generalised additive models, monotonic gradient boosting, scorecards derived from complex models — occupy useful middle ground and are under-used in practice.

The professional discipline is to measure the trade-off rather than assume it. Build the interpretable benchmark first. If the complex model cannot beat it materially, the decision is made for you.

sections.h: Interpretable by design versus explained after the fact
sections.html:
Two fundamentally different strategies, frequently conflated:

  • Intrinsically interpretable models. Logistic regression, scorecards, shallow decision trees, rule sets. The model is the explanation. Nothing can diverge, because there is no separate explanatory artefact.
  • Post-hoc explanation. A complex model is built, then a second technique approximates why it produced a given output. SHAP, LIME and counterfactuals fall here.

The critical difference is that post-hoc explanations are approximations of the model, not descriptions of it. They can be unstable — small input changes producing materially different explanations — and two methods can attribute importance differently for the same prediction. For a regulated adverse decision, that is a genuine exposure.

sections.h: The techniques, and what each is actually for
sections.html:
• SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations). Attributes a prediction to each feature using a game-theoretic allocation. Strengths: consistent, additive, supports both global and local views. Limitations: computationally expensive at scale, and correlated features can distribute credit in ways that mislead a non-technical reader.
  • LIME. Fits a simple local surrogate around one prediction. Strengths: intuitive, model-agnostic, fast. Limitations: sensitive to sampling choices, and explanations can vary between runs — which is difficult to defend if a customer challenges a decision twice.
  • Counterfactual explanations. "Had your total exposure been below X, the application would have been approved." Strengths: directly actionable, closest to what a declined customer actually wants, and naturally aligned with adverse-action reasoning. Limitations: must be constrained to realistic, permissible changes — a counterfactual suggesting the applicant change age or district is both useless and legally hazardous.
  • Global techniques — feature importance, partial dependence, accumulated local effects — describe overall model behaviour for validators and supervisors rather than individual decisions.

For most banking purposes, counterfactuals communicate best to customers and SHAP communicates best to validators. Institutions that pick one technique for all audiences serve none of them well.

The literature review names a failure mode that experienced practitioners recognise immediately: the explanation itself requires expertise to interpret.

A SHAP waterfall plot is meaningful to a data scientist. Presented to a branch manager, a declined customer or a supervisor unfamiliar with the method, it does not explain — it transfers the opacity one level up while creating an appearance of transparency. The institution can now say it provides explanations; nobody outside the modelling team can actually use them.

The practical test

An explanation is adequate only if the intended recipient can act on it or challenge it. A declined applicant should learn what to change. A relationship manager should be able to hold a credible conversation. A validator should be able to identify an unreasonable dependency. A supervisor should be able to assess fairness. If your explanation does none of these for the person receiving it, you have documentation rather than explainability.

Four audiences, four requirements — this is the design discipline the literature calls context-aware explanation design:

  • The customer. Plain language, few factors, actionable. "Your application was declined primarily because of the level of existing borrowing relative to income, and a limited repayment history with us." Counterfactual where possible.
  • Front-line staff. Enough to hold a credible conversation and to recognise when the model may be wrong, plus a defined route to escalate an override.
  • Model validators and risk. Global behaviour, feature dependencies, subgroup performance, stability of explanations, sensitivity analysis.
  • Supervisors, including NRB. Evidence that the model is transparent, explainable, fair and accountable — the framework's stated requirements — supported by documented methodology, validation, monitoring and named accountability.

sections.h: Why implementation fails, and what fixes it
sections.html:
The review is emphatic that the barriers are principally organisational. The failure patterns:

  • Resistance to change — explanation obligations perceived as an impediment to deployment rather than a condition of it.
  • Misalignment between technical teams and business units — data scientists produce explanations that satisfy technical review while business users still cannot use them.
  • No standardised evaluation framework — no agreed definition of what makes an explanation adequate, so adequacy is asserted rather than tested.

The remedies the literature points toward are structural: interdisciplinary collaboration between modelling, business, risk and compliance from design onward; context-aware explanation design as described above; and human-centric governance that treats explanation as a product requirement with acceptance criteria, not a documentation task completed at the end.

Practically: define, before development begins, who must be able to understand what — and test the explanation with those people before the model goes live. An explanation that has never been shown to a branch manager should not be assumed to work for one.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: build the interpretable benchmark first
practitioner.text: Before approving development of a complex model for any regulated decision, require the team to build a well-specified interpretable benchmark — a proper scorecard or constrained model — and report its performance. Two things follow. If the complex model does not beat it materially, you have avoided an unnecessary explainability burden. If it does, you have quantified exactly what you are buying with the added opacity, which is precisely the evidence a supervisor will want to see.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Take one model-assisted decision at your institution and write four explanations of the same declined case: one for the customer, one for the relationship manager, one for a validator, one for a supervisor. Then test the first two on someone in that role who was not involved. Most institutions discover their existing explanation serves only the modelling team — and that discovery is the point of the exercise.

takeaways: A 2026 systematic review of 78 studies finds XAI's barriers are principally organisational, not technical
Measure the accuracy–interpretability trade-off rather than assuming it; build the interpretable benchmark first
Post-hoc explanations approximate the model and can be unstable — intrinsically interpretable models cannot diverge
Counterfactuals communicate best to customers; SHAP communicates best to validators
The 'explaining the explanation' problem transfers opacity upward while appearing transparent
An explanation is adequate only if the recipient can act on it or challenge it
XAI must become an embedded organisational capability with acceptance criteria, not a documentation task

quiz.q: The 2026 systematic literature review on XAI in banking concludes that the principal barriers to adoption are:
opts: Organisational and cultural — resistance to change, business-technical misalignment, and no standardised evaluation frameworks
Purely technical — the algorithms do not work
quiz.fb: Technical challenges are real but the review finds they are compounded by more fundamental organisational barriers, requiring structural change.

quiz.q: Which explanation type is generally most useful to a declined loan applicant?
opts: A counterfactual explanation stating what would need to change for approval
quiz.fb: Counterfactuals are actionable and align naturally with adverse-action reasoning — provided they are constrained to realistic, permissible changes.

quiz.q: The 'explaining the explanation' problem refers to:
opts: Explanations written in a foreign language
Explanations that themselves require expertise to interpret, transferring opacity upward while appearing transparent
quiz.fb: A SHAP plot shown to a branch manager or customer creates the appearance of transparency without delivering usable understanding.

quiz.q: A key limitation of LIME that matters for regulated decisions is:
opts: It cannot be used on tabular data
It requires the source code of the model
Explanations can vary between runs due to sampling, which is hard to defend if a customer challenges a decision twice
quiz.fb: Instability in post-hoc explanations is a genuine exposure where a bank must give a consistent reason for an adverse decision.

quiz.q: Before approving a complex model for a regulated credit decision, best practice is to:
opts: Build a well-specified interpretable benchmark first and quantify what the added opacity buys
Approve it if the vendor's AUC is high
Choose the model with the most parameters
quiz.fb: If the complex model does not beat the interpretable benchmark materially, you avoid an unnecessary explainability burden; if it does, you have evidenced the trade-off.

quiz.q: A counterfactual explanation suggesting an applicant would have been approved 'if you lived in a different district' is:
opts: Useless and legally hazardous — counterfactuals must be constrained to realistic, permissible changes
quiz.fb: Counterfactuals must be restricted to attributes the customer can legitimately change; otherwise they expose the institution to discrimination findings.

finance-advanced.title: Foundation Models, LLMOps & the Modern AI Stack
finance-advanced.summary: Building on external models without losing control
objectives: Distinguish foundation models from large language models and understand what pre-training implies
Evaluate build, buy, customise and fine-tune as strategic options
Understand the modern generative AI stack and how it differs from the predictive AI stack
Design evaluation harnesses and guardrails appropriate to a regulated institution
Manage foundation-model dependency, vendor concentration and version risk
Understand the economics of inference and where cost actually accumulates

sections.h: Foundation models and large language models — the distinction matters
sections.html:
BCG's Banking on Generative AI draws a distinction that is frequently blurred and has procurement consequences:

  • Foundation models (FMs) are pre-trained on large datasets with substantial compute, ready to use without additional training, and applicable to many tasks — generating text or graphics, predicting, or classifying.
  • Large language models (LLMs) are a subset of foundation models that ingest and produce text.

As BCG states plainly, the terms are not interchangeable. The practical significance is that an institution's generative capability may involve models handling documents, images and structured data, not only chat. Procurement, governance and risk frameworks written narrowly around "chatbots" will not cover what is actually deployed.

sections.h: A separate stack, not an extension of the old one
sections.html:
One of the most useful corrections in BCG's analysis is that classic predictive AI and generative AI run on largely separate technology stacks.

  • Predictive stack: data warehouse, feature store, model training pipelines, MLOps, model serving, monitoring. Requires mature, structured data.
  • Generative stack: foundation models (hosted or self-run), embedding models, vector stores, caches, retrieval pipelines, prompt and agent orchestration, guardrails, model abstraction layers. Requires documents more than warehouses.

The only major shared component is the data lake or document store. This is why the common objection — "our data isn't ready for AI" — is only half right. It is decisive for a new credit scorecard. It is much less binding for document processing, policy assistants or drafting support, which can proceed in parallel with data remediation.

sections.h: Build, buy, customise: the strategic decision
sections.html:
The Cambridge data shows what the industry has actually chosen: 63% of industry respondents and 65% of regulators use internal workflows built on external foundation models, though many also customise or develop some systems in-house. Training a foundation model from scratch is not a realistic option for any Nepali institution, and is increasingly not one for most global banks either.

The meaningful options, in ascending order of cost and control:

  1. Prompt engineering on a hosted model. Fastest, cheapest, no training. Surprisingly capable. The correct starting point for almost every use case.
  2. Retrieval-augmented generation. Ground responses in your own documents. Covered in the foundational programme; the default architecture for regulated knowledge work.
  3. Fine-tuning. Adapting a model's behaviour on your own examples. Useful for consistent formatting, house style or a specialised task — rarely for teaching facts, which retrieval does better and updates more easily.
  4. Self-hosted open-weight models. Full data control, no external dependency, higher infrastructure and skills cost. Increasingly viable and relevant where data residency is a hard requirement.

Deeper dive: fine-tuning is usually the wrong first answer

Teams reach for fine-tuning because it feels like real engineering. In practice, most problems attributed to model capability are prompt or retrieval problems. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into weights that then require re-tuning when policy changes, whereas retrieval updates the moment you update the document. Exhaust prompting and retrieval before fine-tuning, and be explicit about what fine-tuning is meant to fix.

sections.h: Evaluation harnesses — validation for systems that produce text
sections.html:
You cannot compute a Gini coefficient for a drafting assistant. Institutional discipline requires an evaluation harness: a fixed, versioned set of representative tasks with known-good answers, run automatically against every model or prompt change.

A workable harness for a banking deployment includes:

  • Golden set. 50–200 real, de-identified cases with agreed correct outputs, curated with the business.
  • Factual grounding checks. Does the output cite retrieved source material, and does the citation genuinely support the claim?
  • Refusal and boundary tests. Does it decline requests it should decline — advice it is not permitted to give, data it should not disclose?
  • Adversarial prompts. Including prompt-injection attempts embedded in documents the system processes.
  • Regression testing. Rerun on every change. Providers update models; behaviour shifts without notice.
  • Human review sampling. A standing percentage of live outputs reviewed and scored, feeding back into the golden set.

The Cambridge study identifies model hallucinations among the most-cited risks by both industry and regulators. An evaluation harness is the operational answer, and it is what a supervisor will ask to see.

Guardrails sit between the model and the user, and between the model and your systems:

  • Input filtering — blocking or redacting customer identifiers before they reach an external model.
  • Output validation — schema checks, forbidden-content checks, and verification that cited sources exist.
  • Tool and action constraints — an assistant able to query balances must not be able to move money.
  • Rate and cost limits — protecting against runaway loops, particularly in agentic systems.
  • Comprehensive logging — prompt, retrieved context, output, model version, user, timestamp. Without this you cannot investigate an incident.

A model abstraction layer — a thin internal interface through which all model calls pass — is worth building early. It makes provider substitution, version pinning, logging and cost control a configuration change rather than a rewrite across dozens of applications.

The Cambridge survey documents a genuine concentration:

  • OpenAI is the most-used foundation model provider — 76% of industry respondents and 48% of regulators.
  • Google follows at 57% of industry, Anthropic at 35% of industry and 33% of vendors, DeepSeek at 15% of industry.
  • In cloud, AWS leads industry at 46%; among regulators using cloud, Azure leads at 39%; and 46% of regulators report using no cloud infrastructure at all.

Concentration creates risks that belong on a risk register, not only in a procurement file: correlated outage across the sector; unilateral changes to model behaviour, pricing or terms; deprecation of a version a live process depends on; and jurisdictional exposure where processing occurs abroad.

Practical mitigations: pin model versions explicitly; maintain a tested fallback provider or self-hosted option for critical paths; keep prompts and retrieval logic portable rather than provider-specific; and negotiate notice periods for material model changes.

Predictive AI concentrates cost in training; generative AI concentrates it in inference — you pay per use, forever. This inverts capital planning, and pilots systematically understate it because pilot volumes are small.

Where cost accumulates, and the levers that matter:

  • Context length. Retrieving twenty documents when three would do multiplies cost on every call. Retrieval quality is a cost lever, not only an accuracy one.
  • Model selection by task. Routing simple classification to a small model and reserving the largest model for genuinely hard reasoning is the single largest saving available.
  • Caching. Repeated or near-identical queries should not trigger repeated inference.
  • Agentic loops. An agent that reasons across multiple steps may make many calls per task — the cost driver examined in Module 6.

Model the cost at realistic production volume before committing, and include it in the business case. An assistant that is delightful at 50 users per day can be indefensible at 5,000.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: build the harness before the pilot
practitioner.text: Insist that any generative AI proposal arrives with its evaluation harness defined — the golden set, who curated it, and the pass thresholds — before the pilot begins. Teams resist this because it delays the demonstration by a fortnight. It is also the only thing that lets you distinguish a genuinely improved system from a differently-phrased one, and the only artefact that will satisfy a supervisor asking how you assure output quality.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: For one generative AI use case in your institution, specify: the four stack components it requires; whether you are prompting, retrieving, fine-tuning or self-hosting and why; twenty golden-set cases you would use to evaluate it; the three guardrails you would implement; and the estimated monthly inference cost at full production volume. If the cost estimate surprises you, that is the module working.

takeaways: Foundation models and LLMs are not interchangeable — LLMs are the text subset of a broader class
Generative AI runs on a separate stack from predictive AI; weak data warehouses do not block document-centric use cases
63% of firms build internal workflows on external foundation models; training from scratch is not a realistic option
Exhaust prompting and retrieval before fine-tuning; retrieval updates instantly, fine-tuning does not
An evaluation harness with a golden set is the operational answer to hallucination risk and what supervisors will request
Vendor concentration is real — OpenAI 76% of industry — requiring version pinning, fallback and portable logic
Generative AI concentrates cost in inference; model routing and retrieval quality are the main cost levers

quiz.q: The relationship between foundation models and large language models is:
opts: LLMs are a subset of foundation models — the ones that ingest and produce text
Foundation models are a subset of LLMs
quiz.fb: BCG is explicit that the terms are not interchangeable. Governance written only around chatbots will not cover document, image and classification models.

quiz.q: An institution has a weak data warehouse. Which conclusion is correct?
opts: No AI work can begin until it is fixed
Only cloud providers can solve this
Generative AI is impossible without a warehouse
It is decisive for a new credit scorecard but much less binding for document processing or policy assistants, which use a different stack
quiz.fb: Generative AI depends on documents, embeddings, vector stores and retrieval — largely a separate stack from the predictive AI data warehouse.

quiz.q: A team proposes fine-tuning a model so it 'knows' the bank's current lending policy. The better approach is usually:
opts: Retrieval-augmented generation, because it updates the moment the policy document changes
Training a foundation model from scratch
quiz.fb: Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into weights requiring re-tuning when policy changes. Retrieval keeps facts external and current.

quiz.q: The primary operational control against hallucination in a regulated deployment is:
opts: An evaluation harness with a versioned golden set, grounding checks and regression testing on every change
quiz.fb: You cannot compute a Gini for a text system. A harness is how you evidence output quality to yourself and to a supervisor.

quiz.q: According to the Cambridge survey, the most-used foundation model provider among industry respondents is:
quiz.fb: OpenAI leads at 76% of industry respondents, followed by Google at 57% and Anthropic at 35% — a concentration that belongs on the risk register.

quiz.q: Compared with predictive AI, generative AI shifts cost toward:
opts: Inference — paid per use, indefinitely, and systematically understated by low-volume pilots
quiz.fb: Inference cost scales with usage and context length. Model routing by task difficulty is typically the largest available saving.

finance-advanced.title: Agentic AI in Banking
finance-advanced.summary: Systems that act, and the controls they demand
objectives: Define agentic AI precisely and distinguish it from assistants and automation
Understand adoption trajectory and why agentic AI is the clearest growth frontier
Describe agent architecture: planning, tools, memory and orchestration
Apply a levels-of-autonomy framework to banking processes
Identify agent-specific failure modes and design controls for them
Determine which banking processes are suitable for agentic treatment and which are not

sections.html:
An assistant responds to a request. An agent pursues a goal: it plans a sequence of steps, invokes tools, observes results, adapts, and continues until the objective is met or it stops. The distinguishing capabilities are planning, tool use, memory and autonomy over multiple steps.

The distinction from traditional automation matters. Robotic process automation follows a fixed script and breaks when the screen changes. An agent determines its own path, which makes it far more capable and considerably harder to govern — because you cannot enumerate in advance every sequence it might take.

The Cambridge 2026 data shows unusually rapid uptake:

  • 52% of industry respondents are already in active adoption of agentic AI, with 23% at Scaling or Transforming and 29% piloting.
  • Fintechs again lead traditional institutions — 57% versus 45%.
  • 81% of industry respondents expect agentic AI to be meaningfully achieved by 2030, making it the clearest growth frontier in AI technology.

The report also notes that GenAI and agentic AI have lower engineering barriers than traditional machine learning methods, which explains the speed: an institution can deploy an agent without the labelled datasets, feature engineering and model training that a predictive model demands. That accessibility is exactly why governance must arrive early rather than after deployment.

Four components, each with control implications:

  • The planner. Decomposes a goal into steps. Typically a language model reasoning about what to do next. Its plan is generated, not fixed, so it must be constrained and logged.
  • Tools. The functions the agent may invoke — query a database, call an API, send an email, create a case, execute a payment. The tool list defines the agent's maximum blast radius. This is the single most important control surface.
  • Memory. Short-term working context plus, sometimes, longer-term storage. Memory introduces a subtle risk: an error recorded early can persist and contaminate later reasoning.
  • The orchestrator. Manages the loop, enforces limits on steps and cost, handles failure, and decides when to stop or escalate.

Multi-agent systems add specialised agents coordinating with one another. Powerful, and materially harder to audit — when an outcome is wrong, determining which agent's reasoning caused it is genuinely difficult.

sections.h: Levels of autonomy — the governance framework
sections.html:
The most useful control concept is to classify each deployment by autonomy level and require approval proportionate to it:

  1. Level 0 — Suggest. The agent proposes; a human performs the action. No system access beyond reading.
  2. Level 1 — Draft and stage. The agent prepares a complete action — a populated case, a drafted response, a proposed journal entry — which a human reviews and releases.
  3. Level 2 — Act within limits. The agent executes autonomously within tightly defined boundaries: value thresholds, customer segments, transaction types. Everything outside escalates.
  4. Level 3 — Act with exception reporting. The agent acts routinely; humans review exceptions and samples after the fact.
  5. Level 4 — Fully autonomous. Appropriate only for reversible, low-materiality, well-bounded processes with strong monitoring.

For any process affecting customer funds, credit decisions, regulatory reporting or financial crime disposition, Level 1 or Level 2 with hard limits is the defensible position today. Level 2 limits should be expressed in the same terms as a delegated authority — because that is exactly what they are.

• Goal misinterpretation. The agent optimises what was asked rather than what was meant. An agent told to reduce open cases may close them without resolution.
  • Compounding error. A wrong conclusion at step two becomes an assumption at steps three through nine. Small initial errors produce large final ones.
  • Runaway loops. The agent retries indefinitely, consuming cost and, worse, repeatedly triggering downstream actions. Hard step and spend limits are mandatory.
  • Tool misuse. Invoking a legitimate tool in an inappropriate context — the correct API, the wrong account.
  • Prompt injection through data. The most serious agentic risk. Instructions concealed in a document, email or web page the agent processes cause it to ignore its constraints. An agent that both reads external content and holds powerful tools is a genuine security exposure.
  • Attribution failure. In multi-agent systems, tracing a bad outcome to a specific decision may be impractical — which undermines both remediation and accountability.

The design rule that follows

Separate reading untrusted content from holding powerful tools. An agent that ingests external documents should have read-only capabilities. An agent with write or transactional authority should operate only on trusted, validated inputs. Combining both in one agent is the architectural equivalent of granting internet-sourced instructions your payment authority.

sections.h: Where agentic AI genuinely fits in banking
sections.html:
Strong candidates share a profile: multi-step, rule-bounded, high-volume, reversible, and with a clear definition of done.

  • Financial crime investigation preparation. Assembling the case file — transaction history, related parties, prior alerts, adverse media, KYC documents — so the investigator begins with a complete picture rather than assembling one. The human still decides.
  • Credit file assembly. Gathering statements, spreads, covenant checks and portfolio context into a structured pack for the analyst.
  • Reconciliation and exception handling. Investigating breaks, proposing resolutions, escalating what it cannot resolve.
  • Regulatory change mapping. Reading a new circular, identifying affected policies and controls, drafting a gap list for compliance review.
  • Customer service resolution within defined limits — the pattern from the foundational programme, with a deterministic core making any binding decision.

Poor candidates: anything irreversible, anything where "done" is a matter of judgement, anything involving a final credit or suspicious-activity determination, and anything where the agent would need to read untrusted external content while holding transactional authority.

1. Tool inventory per agent — documented, approved, minimal.
  2. Hard limits on steps, spend, value and volume, enforced by the orchestrator rather than requested in the prompt.
  3. Complete action logging — every tool call with inputs, outputs and the reasoning that led to it.
  4. A kill switch with named authority to use it, tested rather than assumed.
  5. Human checkpoints at defined materiality thresholds.
  6. Segregation of untrusted-input agents from privileged-tool agents.
  7. Regular sampling of completed agent work, with results feeding the evaluation harness.

The Cambridge study found that respondents cite loss of human oversight among the leading AI risks. Agentic systems are where that concern becomes concrete, and where the controls above are the difference between an oversight failure and a governed capability.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the tool list is the control
practitioner.text: When reviewing any agentic proposal, ask for the tool list before anything else — the exact functions the agent may invoke. Prompts can be circumvented; tools cannot be invoked if they were never granted. An agent that cannot call a payment API cannot make a payment, regardless of what instructions it encounters. Governing the tool list is more effective than governing the prompt, and far easier to evidence.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Select one multi-step process in your department. Specify: the goal an agent would pursue; the exact tools it would need; the autonomy level you would approve and why; the hard limits (steps, value, volume); where a human checkpoint sits; and what would trigger the kill switch. Then apply the segregation test — would this agent read any untrusted external content while holding write authority? If yes, redesign it before proceeding.

takeaways: Agents plan, use tools, hold memory and act over multiple steps — unlike assistants or fixed-script automation
52% of firms are in active agentic adoption and 81% expect it meaningfully achieved by 2030
The tool list defines the agent's maximum blast radius and is the primary control surface
Classify deployments by autonomy level; Level 1 or Level 2 with hard limits is defensible for material processes
Prompt injection through processed content is the most serious agentic risk
Never combine reading untrusted content with holding powerful tools in the same agent
Good candidates are multi-step, rule-bounded, reversible and have a clear definition of done

quiz.q: What distinguishes an agentic system from an AI assistant?
opts: It pursues a goal across multiple steps using planning, tools and memory, adapting as it goes
quiz.fb: Agents determine their own path to a goal, which makes them more capable and harder to govern than fixed-script automation.

quiz.q: The most effective control surface for an agentic deployment is:
opts: The tool list — the exact functions the agent is permitted to invoke
The wording of the system prompt
quiz.fb: Prompts can be circumvented; an agent cannot invoke a tool it was never granted. The tool list defines the maximum blast radius.

quiz.q: An agent processes incoming supplier emails and also holds authority to initiate payments. This design is:
opts: A serious exposure — reading untrusted content must be segregated from holding powerful tools
Safe if the model is large enough
quiz.fb: Prompt injection concealed in processed content could direct the agent's payment authority. Segregation is the architectural rule.

quiz.q: For a process affecting customer funds or credit decisions, the defensible autonomy level today is:
opts: Level 1 or Level 2 with hard limits expressed like a delegated authority
quiz.fb: Draft-and-stage, or act-within-tightly-defined-limits, keeps a human accountable for material outcomes while capturing efficiency.

quiz.q: 'Compounding error' in an agentic system refers to:
opts: An incorrect conclusion at an early step becoming an assumption for all subsequent steps
quiz.fb: Because each step builds on the last, small initial errors can produce large final ones — which is why step limits and checkpoints matter.

quiz.q: According to the Cambridge study, agentic AI adoption among industry respondents currently stands at approximately:
opts: 52% in active adoption, with 81% expecting it meaningfully achieved by 2030
quiz.fb: Rapid uptake reflects lower engineering barriers than traditional ML — which is precisely why governance must arrive early.

finance-advanced.title: Advanced Credit Risk & Capital
finance-advanced.summary: IFRS 9, stress testing, fairness and the regulated credit model
objectives: Apply AI across the credit risk parameter set: PD, LGD and EAD
Understand IFRS 9 expected credit loss and where machine learning legitimately contributes
Understand the role of models in stress testing and scenario analysis
Design champion–challenger programmes that generate defensible evidence
Conduct rigorous fairness testing appropriate to a regulated lender
Understand reject inference, through-the-cycle versus point-in-time, and other advanced modelling considerations

sections.html:
Advanced credit work requires precision about which quantity is being modelled, because each has different data requirements and regulatory sensitivity:

  • Probability of default (PD) — the likelihood of default within a defined horizon. The most modelled and most data-rich parameter.
  • Loss given default (LGD) — the proportion of exposure lost when default occurs. Depends on collateral, recovery process and time to recovery. Data is scarcer because only defaulted accounts contribute, and recovery outcomes take years to observe.
  • Exposure at default (EAD) — the amount outstanding at the moment of default, which for revolving facilities requires modelling drawdown behaviour as a borrower deteriorates.

Machine learning has contributed most to PD, where data is plentiful. LGD and EAD remain harder, and models there are typically simpler by necessity — a point worth remembering when a vendor claims uniform improvement across all three.

IFRS 9 requires forward-looking expected credit loss provisioning rather than incurred loss, with exposures allocated across three stages by change in credit risk since origination, and lifetime ECL recognised from Stage 2 onward.

This creates specific modelling demands where AI can contribute — and specific constraints:

  • Lifetime PD term structures rather than a twelve-month point estimate.
  • Significant increase in credit risk (SICR) determination — the trigger for Stage 2. Behavioural models can inform this, but the criteria must be explainable and consistently applied.
  • Forward-looking macroeconomic scenarios with probability weights, requiring the model to respond sensibly to economic inputs.

The constraint that matters: ECL flows directly into the financial statements and is audited. This makes calibration and explainability non-negotiable, and it is why many institutions retain interpretable models for ECL while using machine learning for early warning and origination. That is a defensible architecture, not a failure of ambition.

Stress testing asks how the portfolio behaves under adverse conditions. It exposes a structural weakness in data-driven models: a model trained on benign conditions has never observed the scenario you most need it to predict.

Practical implications:

  • Extrapolation is unreliable. Complex models can behave erratically outside their training range. Interpretable models with economically sensible coefficients often extrapolate more defensibly, even if they fit historical data less tightly.
  • Sensitivity must be plausible. If unemployment rises three points, default rates should move in a direction and magnitude a credit officer finds reasonable. Test this explicitly.
  • Overlays are expected here. Where history is unrepresentative, documented judgemental adjustment is legitimate — subject to the governance in Module 3.

SAS's research quotes a chief risk officer at Millennium BCP describing models developed "to help us better prepare for adverse scenarios in the next five years... so if an economic crisis arises, we can more effectively mitigate the effects of a rise in defaults." That is the correct framing: preparation and mitigation, not prediction of the unpredictable.

Champion–challenger is the mechanism that lets an institution adopt better models without unmanaged risk. Done well it requires discipline:

  1. The champion continues to decide. The challenger runs in parallel, scoring the same applications without influencing outcomes.
  2. Compare on the same population over the same period — differences in either invalidate the comparison.
  3. Allow sufficient outcome maturity. Judging a credit model before the outcome window has elapsed measures nothing. For most retail portfolios this means twelve to eighteen months minimum.
  4. Pre-specify the promotion criteria. What improvement, on which metrics, sustained over what period, justifies switching? Agreeing this after seeing results invites motivated reasoning.
  5. Evaluate beyond discrimination — calibration, stability, fairness across segments, and explainability adequacy all form part of the decision.

A rigorous champion–challenger programme is also the strongest possible evidence to a supervisor that model change is controlled rather than opportunistic.

sections.h: Fairness testing for a regulated lender
sections.html:
Module 3 of the foundational programme introduced proxy discrimination. At an advanced level, three refinements matter:

  • Fairness definitions conflict mathematically. Demographic parity (equal approval rates), equalised odds (equal error rates) and calibration within groups generally cannot all hold simultaneously when base rates differ. This is a proven result, not an engineering shortfall. The institution must therefore choose and justify a fairness criterion rather than claim to satisfy all of them.
  • Test error rates, not only approval rates. Two groups can have identical approval rates while the model is markedly less accurate for one — which is a different and often more serious harm.
  • Proxy detection is empirical. Attempt to predict the protected attribute from the model's inputs. If it is predictable with meaningful accuracy, proxies are present and must be addressed.

NRB's guidelines require AI applications to be fair and non-discriminatory. Documented, repeated fairness testing with a justified criterion is how that requirement is evidenced. Testing once at build time and never again does not meet it.

• Reject inference. Origination models are trained only on approved applicants, whose performance is observed — a systematically biased sample, since the worst applicants were declined. Reject inference techniques attempt to correct this. They are imperfect and assumption-heavy; the honest position is to use them, document the assumptions, and remember that the model's view of rejected populations is inferred rather than observed.
  • Through-the-cycle versus point-in-time. TTC estimates aim for stability across the economic cycle and suit capital; PIT estimates reflect current conditions and suit IFRS 9 and pricing. Confusing the two produces either volatile capital or unresponsive provisions.
  • Survivorship and selection effects. Behavioural models built on customers who remained with the institution exclude those who left — often the dissatisfied or the refinanced.
  • Definition consistency. "Default" must mean the same thing in the model, the policy, the regulatory return and the financial statements. Divergence here is a common and material finding.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: ask which fairness definition
practitioner.text: When a team reports that a credit model has been "tested for fairness", ask which definition was used and why that one was chosen. Because demographic parity, equalised odds and within-group calibration cannot generally hold simultaneously, an unqualified claim of fairness signals that the trade-off was never confronted. A team that answers "we prioritised equalised odds because the cost of unequal error rates in this portfolio is higher, and here is the documented rationale" is one that understands the problem.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Take your institution's principal credit model. Document: which parameter it estimates (PD, LGD or EAD); whether it is TTC or PIT and whether that matches its use; how SICR is determined if it feeds IFRS 9; whether reject inference was applied and on what assumptions; which fairness definition was tested, when, and with what result; and whether "default" is defined identically in the model, policy and regulatory return. Every gap is a finding worth raising.

takeaways: PD, LGD and EAD have different data availability; machine learning has contributed most to PD
ECL is audited and enters the financial statements, making calibration and explainability non-negotiable
Models trained on benign conditions extrapolate unreliably — stress testing requires plausible sensitivity and documented overlays
Champion–challenger requires the same population, mature outcomes and pre-specified promotion criteria
Fairness definitions conflict mathematically; the institution must choose and justify one
Test error rates across groups, not only approval rates
Reject inference is assumption-heavy; TTC and PIT serve different purposes and must not be confused

quiz.q: Why do many institutions retain interpretable models for IFRS 9 expected credit loss while using machine learning for early warning?
opts: ECL is audited and enters the financial statements, so calibration and explainability are non-negotiable
Interpretable models are always more accurate
quiz.fb: This is a defensible architecture: the audited provision requires numerically correct, explainable output, while early warning tolerates more complexity.

quiz.q: A team reports their credit model is 'fair'. The correct challenge is:
opts: Accept the finding and move on
Ask which fairness definition was used and why, since demographic parity, equalised odds and within-group calibration cannot generally all hold
quiz.fb: The impossibility of simultaneously satisfying these definitions when base rates differ is a proven result. An unqualified fairness claim means the trade-off was never confronted.

quiz.q: Reject inference addresses which problem?
opts: Origination models are trained only on approved applicants, a systematically biased sample
quiz.fb: Performance is observed only for those approved. Reject inference attempts to correct this, but it is assumption-heavy and must be documented as inferred.

quiz.q: Confusing through-the-cycle and point-in-time estimates typically produces:
opts: Either volatile capital or unresponsive provisions, depending on which is misapplied
quiz.fb: TTC suits capital because it is stable across the cycle; PIT suits IFRS 9 and pricing because it reflects current conditions.

quiz.q: In a champion–challenger programme, promotion criteria should be:
opts: Pre-specified — what improvement, on which metrics, sustained over what period
quiz.fb: Agreeing criteria after seeing results invites motivated reasoning. Pre-specification is also the strongest evidence to a supervisor that change is controlled.

quiz.q: A model trained entirely on benign economic conditions is used for stress testing. The principal concern is:
opts: It has never observed the scenario it is being asked to predict, and complex models extrapolate unreliably
quiz.fb: Extrapolation beyond the training range is unreliable. Test that sensitivities are economically plausible and document judgemental overlays.

finance-advanced.title: Financial Crime at Scale: Graph & Network Intelligence
finance-advanced.summary: Entity resolution, network analytics and privacy-preserving collaboration
objectives: Apply graph analytics to financial crime beyond transaction-level monitoring
Understand entity resolution and why it determines detection capability
Understand typology discovery and unsupervised detection of unknown patterns
Evaluate privacy-enhancing technologies for cross-institution collaboration
Design a target financial crime architecture appropriate to a Nepali institution
Understand model risk considerations specific to financial crime systems

sections.h: Why the network is the unit of analysis
sections.html:
The foundational programme introduced graph analytics for mule networks and layering. At an advanced level, the shift is conceptual: in sophisticated financial crime, the network is the criminal artefact. Individual transactions are deliberately unremarkable — that is the design intent of structuring.

Formally, accounts and parties become nodes and transfers become edges, with attributes on both. Detection then draws on established network measures:

  • Centrality — accounts through which disproportionate flow passes, characteristic of collectors and hubs.
  • Community detection — densely connected clusters transacting far more with each other than with the wider network.
  • Path and cycle analysis — funds returning to origin through intermediaries, or moving through a chain within a compressed timeframe.
  • Temporal patterns — synchronised behaviour across nominally unrelated accounts, a strong signal of coordination.
  • Shared attributes — device identifiers, phone numbers, addresses, beneficiaries or employers linking supposedly independent customers.

Given the scale of remittance flows and the rapid growth of digital wallets in Nepal, shared-attribute and temporal analysis are particularly productive: mule recruitment concentrates where accounts are numerous, newly opened and individually low-value.

Network analytics is worthless if the same person appears as four unconnected nodes. Entity resolution — determining which records refer to the same real-world person or business — is the prerequisite capability, and it is genuinely hard in the Nepali context:

  • Transliteration variance between Devanagari and Roman script, with multiple valid romanisations of the same name.
  • Name ordering and patronymics applied inconsistently across systems.
  • Address formats that are descriptive rather than standardised.
  • Identifier gaps where citizenship number, PAN and national ID are captured inconsistently across products and vintages.

Machine learning contributes through probabilistic matching — phonetic similarity, edit distance, contextual signals such as shared addresses or devices — producing a match confidence rather than a binary answer. Institutions should hold two thresholds: a high one for automatic linkage and a lower one routing candidate matches to human review.

Entity resolution improvement typically delivers more detection uplift per rupee than any new detection model. It is unglamorous and it is where the leverage sits.

sections.h: Finding typologies nobody has written a rule for
sections.html:
Supervised models learn known patterns from labelled cases. Their structural limitation is that they cannot detect a typology absent from the training data — and novel typologies are precisely what causes losses.

Unsupervised and semi-supervised methods address this gap:

  • Anomaly detection — flagging behaviour that does not resemble any established pattern, whether or not it resembles known crime.
  • Peer-group analysis — comparing a customer against genuinely similar customers rather than a portfolio average. A cash pattern normal for a retail merchant is abnormal for a salaried professional.
  • Behavioural change detection — a dormant account suddenly transacting actively, or a stable pattern shifting abruptly, is often more informative than any absolute threshold.
  • Graph embeddings — representing each node's network position numerically so that structurally similar accounts can be identified even when their transactions differ.

These methods generate hypotheses rather than conclusions. Their proper output is a prioritised queue for skilled investigators, and their value depends entirely on investigator capacity to work it.

Financial crime crosses institutional boundaries; detection data does not. A mule network spanning five banks is visible to none of them individually. Several technologies address this without pooling raw customer data:

  • Federated learning — institutions jointly train a model while data remains local; only model updates are shared.
  • Secure multi-party computation — parties jointly compute a result without revealing their inputs.
  • Homomorphic encryption — computation performed directly on encrypted data. Powerful, still computationally expensive.
  • Privacy-preserving record linkage — determining whether two institutions hold records for the same entity without disclosing the underlying identifiers.

These are technically mature enough to matter and, in most markets, blocked by legal and governance questions rather than by engineering. For Nepal, this is properly a sector-level conversation involving NRB and the Financial Information Unit rather than something an individual bank can resolve alone. It is worth raising precisely because the coordination barrier, not the technology, is the obstacle.

A defensible financial crime architecture layers capabilities so that each does what it is best at:

  1. Deterministic rules for regulatory thresholds and mandatory reporting — transparent, auditable, non-negotiable.
  2. Entity resolution beneath everything, continuously improved.
  3. Supervised models scoring and prioritising alerts against known typologies.
  4. Unsupervised detection surfacing novel behaviour the rules and supervised models would miss.
  5. Network analytics assessing structure across linked entities.
  6. Investigator workbench — enriched, assembled cases with the context already gathered (a strong agentic use case, per Module 6).
  7. Governed feedback — investigation outcomes returning as training data, with controls against reinforcing existing blind spots.

sections.h: Model risk in financial crime systems
sections.html:
Financial crime models carry risk characteristics that differ from credit models and deserve explicit treatment:

  • The label is unreliable. "Not reported" does not mean "not criminal" — it may mean not detected. Models trained on historical dispositions learn to reproduce past detection capability, including its blind spots.
  • Adversarial drift. Unlike credit risk, the population actively adapts to evade detection. A model's performance decays because criminals learn it, not merely because conditions change.
  • Feedback loops. If the model directs attention to certain profiles, cases will be found there, confirming the model — while other typologies remain unexamined. Deliberate random sampling outside the model's priorities is a necessary counterweight.
  • Suppression risk. Alert suppression reduces workload but, if wrongly calibrated, systematically hides a category of activity. Suppression rules require the same governance as detection rules, and periodic review of what they excluded.

Filing decisions and customer exit remain human, accountable determinations. AI's role is directing scarce investigative capacity — which, given the false-positive burden documented in the foundational programme, is transformative enough.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: fix entity resolution first
practitioner.text: Before commissioning any new detection model, measure your entity resolution quality: take 200 customers known to hold multiple relationships and check how many are correctly linked across core, cards, digital and loans. Institutions are routinely shocked by the result. Improving entity resolution typically lifts detection more than a new model would, costs less, and simultaneously improves credit, marketing and customer service.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Design a network-analytics pilot for your institution. Specify: which entities and relationships form the graph; which shared attributes you can actually link on today; which network measure you would start with and why; how a flagged network would reach an investigator; and what deliberate random sampling you would run outside the model's priorities to detect its blind spots. Note explicitly which data you would need but do not currently hold reliably.

takeaways: In sophisticated financial crime the network is the criminal artefact; individual transactions are designed to look ordinary
Entity resolution is the prerequisite capability and usually the highest-return investment
Transliteration, name ordering and inconsistent identifiers make entity resolution genuinely hard in Nepal
Unsupervised methods detect typologies no rule anticipated, but produce hypotheses requiring investigator capacity
Privacy-enhancing technologies enable cross-institution detection; the barrier is legal and coordinative, not technical
Financial crime labels are unreliable, populations adapt adversarially, and feedback loops entrench blind spots
Random sampling outside model priorities is a necessary counterweight to feedback loops

quiz.q: Before commissioning a new financial crime detection model, the highest-return investment is usually:
opts: Improving entity resolution so the same person is correctly linked across systems
quiz.fb: Network analytics is worthless if one person appears as four unconnected nodes. Entity resolution also improves credit, marketing and service simultaneously.

quiz.q: Why can supervised models alone not address novel money-laundering typologies?
opts: They learn only patterns present in labelled training data, so they cannot detect a typology never previously observed
quiz.fb: Novel typologies are precisely what causes losses. Unsupervised and anomaly methods surface behaviour that fits no established pattern.

quiz.q: A distinctive model risk in financial crime, compared with credit risk, is:
opts: Adversarial drift — the population actively adapts to evade detection, so performance decays because criminals learn the model
quiz.fb: Credit populations change with conditions; criminal populations change deliberately in response to your controls.

quiz.q: Federated learning allows institutions to:
opts: Pool all raw customer data centrally
Jointly train a model while data remains local, sharing only model updates
quiz.fb: Privacy-enhancing technologies enable collaboration without pooling raw data. In most markets the barrier is legal and coordinative rather than technical.

quiz.q: 'Feedback loops' in financial crime models create the risk that:
opts: Attention concentrates where the model already looks, confirming itself while other typologies go unexamined
quiz.fb: Cases are found where you look. Deliberate random sampling outside the model's priorities is the counterweight that reveals blind spots.

quiz.q: In an AML context, a historical label of 'not reported' means:
opts: The alert was a false positive
Possibly not detected — labels reflect past detection capability including its blind spots
quiz.fb: Training on historical dispositions teaches the model to reproduce previous detection capability, blind spots included.

finance-advanced.title: Enterprise Governance & the Target Operating Model
finance-advanced.summary: Structures, decision rights and the organisation AI requires
objectives: Design an AI governance structure with unambiguous decision rights
Apply the three lines of defence to AI without duplicating existing risk functions
Choose between centralised, federated and hub-and-spoke operating models
Build the policy stack a supervisor would expect to see
Understand talent composition, capability building and the Centre of Excellence
Address the cultural barriers that defeat well-designed frameworks

sections.h: Governance as an enabler, not a brake
sections.html:
The evidence is unambiguous that governance accelerates rather than impedes scaling. EY's research found that more than 70% of large global banks have integrated AI governance into their group-wide risk management frameworks, and that among banks deploying generative AI at scale, more than 80% have established cross-functional AI governance committees or "control towers". Most tellingly, one global commercial bank tripled its number of AI applications without a proportional increase in model-related compliance incidents after implementing a group-level framework.

The Cambridge study reinforces the demand side: clearer regulatory guidance is ranked a top priority by 69% of industry, 67% of vendors and 79% of regulators. Institutions are not resisting governance; they are asking for clarity.

sections.h: Decision rights — the part most frameworks omit
sections.html:
Most AI policies describe principles. Few specify who may decide what. A workable scheme states, for each decision, the accountable role and the evidence required:

  • Approve AI strategy and risk appetite — Board, on recommendation of the executive committee.
  • Approve a Tier 1 model into production — AI or model risk committee, on evidence of independent validation.
  • Approve a Tier 2 model — delegated to the business owner with risk sign-off.
  • Approve a generative AI use case involving customer data — joint approval of information governance and the business owner.
  • Approve an agentic deployment above Level 1 autonomy — AI committee, with documented tool list and limits.
  • Suspend a model in production — named individual, unilaterally, without waiting for a committee.
  • Accept a validation finding as remediated — validation function, not the model owner.

That last item prevents the most common governance failure: the team that built the model deciding its own findings have been addressed.

sections.h: Three lines of defence, applied to AI
sections.html:
AI risk should sit inside existing enterprise risk management rather than beside it. Oxford's research is explicit that AI risk management should not be separate from enterprise risk management, and that the last line of defence will remain human.

  • First line — business and development. Owns the model, its appropriate use, its performance and its customer outcomes. Runs day-to-day monitoring.
  • Second line — risk and compliance. Owns the framework, tiering, independent validation, challenge and aggregate reporting. Must be resourced with people who genuinely understand the models; a second line that cannot challenge technically is ceremonial.
  • Third line — internal audit. Assures that the framework operates as documented. Audits the process, not the mathematics.

Deeper dive: the second-line capability problem

The binding constraint in most institutions is second-line technical capability. If validation cannot interrogate a gradient-boosted model, examine a calibration curve or evaluate an explanation's adequacy, then validation becomes documentation review and the control is nominal. Options are to recruit, to build through structured development, or to buy independent validation — but pretending the capability exists when it does not is the single most dangerous position an institution can hold.

Three operating models, each with a defensible use:

  • Centralised. A single team builds all AI. Strong consistency and control; becomes a bottleneck and drifts from business context. Appropriate at low maturity, where scarce expertise must be concentrated.
  • Federated. Business units build their own with central standards. Fast and contextual; risks duplication, inconsistency and uneven quality. Appropriate at high maturity with strong standards.
  • Hub-and-spoke. A central Centre of Excellence owns platforms, standards, tooling, validation and scarce specialists, while embedded practitioners sit in business units. Most institutions converge here.

Oxford's research adds a caution that matters: introducing central coordination after a period of free experimentation risks "frustrating key individuals", and notes that firms report retention of talent, not just attraction, becoming front of mind. Centralise the standards and the platform; avoid centralising all the interesting work.

EY's finding on composition remains the practical benchmark: in high-return banks, 40–50% of AI team members come from business rather than purely technical backgrounds, and institutions with mature AI talent systems cut the cycle from project approval to launch by 30–50%.

A supervisor examining your institution will expect a coherent documentary hierarchy:

  1. AI policy — board-approved. Scope, principles, risk appetite, accountability, prohibited uses.
  2. Model risk management standard — inventory, tiering, development, validation, monitoring, retirement.
  3. Acceptable use policy for generative AI — what staff may and may not do, and with which approved tools. This is the cheapest and most urgent document most institutions lack.
  4. Data and privacy standards — consent, purpose limitation, retention, cross-border transfer, aligned to the Privacy Act (2075) and NRB requirements.
  5. Third-party and outsourcing standard — due diligence, contractual minimums, exit, concentration limits.
  6. Agentic AI standard — autonomy levels, tool approval, limits, logging, kill-switch authority.
  7. Procedures and templates — validation report format, model documentation template, monitoring pack, incident process.

Templates matter more than they appear to. A standard validation report format makes quality visible and comparable across models, and makes gaps obvious rather than negotiable.

Capability is built through structure rather than enthusiasm:

  • Segment the audience. Board and executive need enough to govern; business leaders need enough to specify and challenge; practitioners need working fluency; specialists need depth. A single training programme serves none of them well.
  • Make AI literacy part of professional development rather than a one-off event — BCG's guidance is explicit that organisations should embed AI literacy in professional development as roles evolve.
  • Train challenge, not just use. Staff must be able to recognise when output is wrong and be genuinely empowered to override it. This is the operational antidote to automation bias.
  • Rotate people through the CoE so capability diffuses into the business rather than concentrating permanently.
  • Retain deliberately. The people you train become externally marketable. Career path, interesting work and recognition matter more than incremental salary.

sections.h: The cultural barriers that defeat good frameworks
sections.html:
The XAI literature review identified organisational and cultural barriers as more fundamental than technical ones. The same applies to governance generally. The recurring failures:

  • Governance experienced as an obstacle rather than a condition of deployment. Countered by making approval paths fast, predictable and proportionate — a Tier 3 tool should not face Tier 1 process.
  • Business–technical misalignment — models built to technical specifications that satisfy no business need. Countered by joint accountability and the 40–50% business composition benchmark.
  • Deployment as the only rewarded outcome. If nobody is ever thanked for stopping a project, unsafe projects proceed. Celebrate a well-reasoned stop publicly at least once.
  • Silence on employment. The Cambridge data offers a usefully balanced position: around two-thirds of industry respondents expect a net increase in jobs, roughly 25% expect significant reskilling, and 24% expect a net reduction. Saying this plainly is better than allowing rumour to fill the vacuum.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: publish the decision-rights table
practitioner.text: Produce a single page listing every AI-related decision, the accountable role, and the evidence required — then circulate it. Most governance failures are not disagreements about principle; they are ambiguity about who decides. A published decision-rights table resolves more disputes than a fifty-page policy, and it is the first artefact a supervisor can use to test whether your framework is real.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Draft the decision-rights table for your institution covering the seven decisions listed in this module. For each, name the accountable role, the required evidence, and the escalation path. Identify which of the seven currently has no clear owner — that gap is your most urgent governance action, and it costs nothing to close.

finance-advanced.title: Systemic Risk, Financial Stability & the Regulatory Frontier
finance-advanced.summary: What AI means for the financial system, and how regulation is responding
objectives: Understand AI's implications for financial stability at system rather than firm level
Explain model herding, uniformity and network connectedness as stability risks
Understand third-party and foundation-model concentration as a systemic exposure
Compare emerging regulatory models internationally
Understand how supervisors themselves are adopting AI, and what that implies
Apply this system-level perspective to Nepal's context and NRB's framework

sections.h: From firm risk to system risk
sections.html:
Every preceding module has considered risk to your institution. This module considers risk to the financial system — the perspective a central bank takes, and one that senior bankers are expected to understand.

The Bank for International Settlements working paper Intelligent financial system: how AI is transforming finance (Aldasoro, Gambacorta, Korinek, Shreeti and Stein, 2024) provides the most rigorous available treatment. Its framing is elegant: the financial system exists to process dispersed information and aggregate it into price signals that coordinate the economy. Advances in information processing have repeatedly transformed finance; AI is the latest and possibly the most consequential.

The paper examines four functions — financial intermediation, insurance, asset management and payments — and assesses implications for financial stability and prudential policy.

The BIS analysis identifies the core stability concern directly. Even early rule-based computer trading systems produced cascade effects and herding — the 1987 US stock market crash being the canonical example. With machine learning, the paper argues, the risks of uniformity, model herding and network connectedness have only compounded.

The mechanism is straightforward and worth stating precisely:

  • Institutions increasingly use similar models, often built on the same foundation models, trained on overlapping data, procured from the same small set of vendors.
  • Similar models reach similar conclusions from similar inputs.
  • Similar conclusions produce correlated actions — tightening credit to the same segments, selling the same assets, restricting the same customers — at the same moment.
  • Correlated actions amplify whatever movement triggered them.

The paper adds a specific generative-AI dimension: co-pilots and robo-advising can make decisions more homogeneous, potentially adding to systemic risk. If every credit analyst in a market is assisted by the same model, drafting from the same reasoning patterns, the diversity of judgement that historically dampened cycles is quietly reduced.

A second concern in the BIS paper deserves particular attention from anyone who will interact with a supervisor: the proliferation of complex interactions and the inherent lack of explainability makes it difficult to spot market manipulation or financial stability risks in time.

This inverts the usual framing of explainability. It is normally discussed as a consumer-protection and conduct issue — can you explain a decline to an applicant? The BIS point is that opacity is also a macroprudential problem. A supervisor cannot detect emerging systemic patterns if the decisions producing them cannot be interpreted, and the speed of automated decisioning removes the friction that historically gave authorities time to intervene.

Module 5 discussed vendor concentration as an institutional risk. At system level it becomes something more serious. Recall the Cambridge findings: OpenAI used by 76% of industry respondents, Google by 57%, with AWS leading cloud at 46%, and 63% of industry building internal workflows on external foundation models.

Concentration of this degree creates exposures that no individual institution can diversify away:

  • Correlated operational failure. A single provider outage simultaneously degrades many institutions.
  • Correlated model failure. A flaw or behavioural change in a widely used model propagates across the sector at once.
  • Cross-border dependency. Critical financial infrastructure depending on providers outside the jurisdiction, beyond the supervisor's reach.
  • Substitutability limits. The concentration exists partly because genuine alternatives are few.

For a small market such as Nepal this is sharper still: the entire banking sector could plausibly depend on two or three foreign providers, with no domestic alternative and limited negotiating power.

sections.h: Two scenarios for the real economy
sections.html:
The BIS paper also examines spillovers from the real economy, presenting two scenarios:

  • The benign scenario. Widespread AI adoption produces broad productivity gains with largely manageable effects — higher output, gradual labour reallocation, improved credit quality as firms become more productive.
  • The disruptive scenario. Significant labour-market displacement occurs faster than reallocation, with consequences for household income, consumer credit performance and demand.

For a bank, the second scenario is a credit risk question, not a technology one: which segments of your portfolio are exposed to occupations most susceptible to displacement? Very few institutions have examined their portfolio through this lens, and it is a legitimate and forward-looking stress scenario to propose.

The BIS paper proposes general principles for AI regulation built on social well-being, transparency, accountability, fairness, privacy protection, safety, human oversight and robustness, and compares regulatory models across the United States, the European Union and China — concluding with an urgent call for international coordination on integrating AI into the global financial system.

The broad picture practitioners should carry:

  • European Union. Comprehensive, risk-tiered legislation with heightened obligations for high-risk uses including credit scoring for individuals.
  • United States. Supervisory guidance and existing law applied to AI — model risk management, fair lending, consumer protection — rather than a single AI statute.
  • China. Directive, application-specific rules issued rapidly alongside active state promotion of adoption.
  • Convergence. Despite differing instruments, supervisors everywhere ask the same four questions: who is accountable, can you explain it, is it fair, and are you monitoring it.

Nepal Rastra Bank's Artificial Intelligence Guidelines sit recognisably within this convergence — board accountability, risk classification, explainability, fairness, privacy aligned to the Privacy Act (2075), consent and opt-out, and embedded ongoing monitoring. An institution that builds to the four convergent questions will be well positioned as NRB's expectations develop. As always, work from the current published text and confirm with your compliance function.

The Cambridge study surveyed 130 central banks and financial regulators, and the findings shape what supervision will look like:

  • 48% remain in the Exploring stage or are not engaged with AI at all; 33% are piloting and 18% scaling.
  • Only 20% report advanced adoption, against 40% of industry.
  • 24% of regulators use no foundation models, and 46% report using no cloud infrastructure at all.
  • 79% rank clearer regulatory guidance as a top priority — the highest of any group.

Two implications follow. First, supervisory capability will lag industry capability for some years, which places more weight on institutions' own governance rather than less. Second, the gap is closing — and supervisory technology will eventually allow authorities to analyse far more than they can today. Institutions whose documentation is genuinely in order will find this unremarkable; others will not.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: ask the herding question
practitioner.text: At your next risk committee, ask one question: "If every bank in Nepal used a model similar to ours, trained on similar data, what would happen in a downturn?" The answer is that they would tighten simultaneously, on the same segments, at the same moment — amplifying the contraction. It is not your institution's job to solve systemic risk, but it is your job to understand that your model's behaviour is correlated with your competitors', and to say so when the board asks whether AI has made the bank safer.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: Conduct a concentration assessment for your institution: list every external AI dependency — foundation model providers, cloud, vendor models embedded in core systems — and for each record what happens to which business process if it becomes unavailable for 48 hours, whether a tested alternative exists, and where processing occurs geographically. Then answer the BIS displacement question: which segments of your loan portfolio are concentrated in occupations most exposed to automation?
