finance-advanced.title: Value Realisation: From Pilots to P&L
finance-advanced.summary: Measuring, capturing and defending the economics of AI
objectives: Understand why most institutions struggle to evidence AI value
Build a value measurement framework linking AI activity to financial outcomes
Use the efficiency ratio as a forward-looking indicator of AI maturity
Understand the investment threshold effect and what it implies for budgeting
Manage AI as a portfolio rather than a set of projects
Avoid the efficiency trap and the double-counting of benefits

sections.h: The measurement problem is real and widespread
sections.html:
The Cambridge data is candid about this. 55% of industry respondents and 63% of surveyed regulators find it difficult to measure the value of AI deployment — rising to 76% among large financial institutions.

Note the direction: the largest institutions find it hardest. Complexity, attribution across many contributing factors, and long chains between an AI intervention and a financial outcome all work against clean measurement. This is not incompetence; it is a genuinely difficult attribution problem that must nevertheless be solved, because unmeasured value cannot be defended at budget time.

Work through four levels, each closer to the P&L:

  1. Activity. Models deployed, users onboarded, queries handled. Necessary for management, worthless as value evidence. Most reporting stops here.
  2. Operational outcome. Time to decision, cost per file, alert precision, straight-through processing rate, error rate. Measurable and directly attributable, provided a baseline exists.
  3. Business outcome. Approval rates at constant risk, loss rates at constant approval, cross-sell conversion, attrition, cases investigated per analyst. Requires controlling for confounds.
  4. Financial outcome. Revenue, cost, impairment, capital, efficiency ratio. The only level a board ultimately accepts — and reachable only if the preceding levels are instrumented.

The practical discipline is to define, before deployment, one metric at each level and the mechanism linking them. A project that cannot articulate that chain has not been thought through, whatever its technical merit.

sections.h: The efficiency ratio as an AI maturity indicator
sections.html:
PwC makes an argument worth adopting: the efficiency ratio — cost as a proportion of income — is evolving from a backward-looking performance measure into "the most telling forward-looking indicator of your bank's ability to leverage AI innovation to compete, grow and endure."

Their Strategy& analysis concludes that institutions fully embracing AI could achieve up to a 15-percentage-point improvement in their efficiency ratio, through dual effects: revenue growth from better targeting, and cost transformation through intelligent automation.

Its value as a management metric is that it is unavoidably honest. It cannot be improved by activity, pilots or announcements. It moves only if income rises or cost falls, and it captures both sides of the AI thesis simultaneously. An institution claiming AI transformation whose efficiency ratio has not moved over three years has a claim worth examining.

One of the more actionable findings in the Cambridge study concerns the relationship between spend and outcome:

  • 62% of organisations spending more than USD 100,000 annually on AI have reached advanced maturity, and 62% of that group report increased profitability — compared with 39% among lower-spending organisations.
  • Overall, 40% of respondents report increased profitability from AI while 43% report no change.
  • Fintechs again outperform: 56% report higher profitability versus 34% of traditional financial institutions.

Read alongside the earlier finding that 53% of respondents spend under USD 100,000 yet report high GenAI and agentic maturity, a nuanced picture emerges. Modest spend can buy capability; sustained spend above a threshold is associated with profitability. The gap between the two is the cost of scaling — integration, change management, governance and monitoring — which is precisely what Oxford's practitioner observed when noting that 60–70% of use-case spend has nothing to do with AI itself but with foundational integration.

For a Nepali institution the practical implication is encouraging: the entry threshold is low, but budget honestly for the integration layer or capability will not convert into profit.

sections.h: Two traps that destroy business cases
sections.html:
The efficiency trap

Oxford's research records a practitioner describing business cases built on "incremental gains on automations, something like 5–15% of every human doing an ops job," tallying to substantial annual savings — and then: "in the real world, we couldn't remove those humans from the system. So most people who put in an AI business case failed to deliver it." Time saved is not money saved unless roles are redesigned or headcount actually changes. State explicitly what the freed capacity will be used for.

The double-counting trap. When several initiatives each claim efficiency in the same function, the same saving is counted repeatedly and the aggregate becomes fictional. Oxford's recommended remedy is to evaluate AI initiatives programmatically as well as case by case — which both prevents double counting and allows enabling investments that generate no standalone return to be funded on the strength of the programme.

Individual business cases produce a collection of local optima. Portfolio management produces capability. A workable structure:

  • Balance horizons. Roughly: 60% near-term efficiency with measurable payback, 30% capability building with indirect return, 10% exploratory. Adjust to appetite, but hold the discipline that not everything must have a standalone business case.
  • Fund enabling infrastructure at portfolio level — data platform, feature store, model serving, monitoring, evaluation harness. These fail every individual ROI test and make everything else possible.
  • Track reuse. EY reports an institution reaching over 50% model reuse and 30–40% lower marginal cost per use case through a centralised platform, achieving measurable returns within 18–24 months. Reuse rate is the clearest single indicator that you are building capability rather than accumulating projects.
  • Review and terminate. A portfolio requires the discipline to stop things. Institutions that never cancel are not managing a portfolio.

A credible quarterly AI report to a board contains, on one page:

  1. Portfolio position — initiatives by stage, with movement since last quarter.
  2. Financial outcomes realised — against baselines, with attribution assumptions stated.
  3. Efficiency ratio trajectory, with commentary on AI's contribution.
  4. Risk position — models by tier, validation status, incidents, monitoring exceptions.
  5. Capability indicators — reuse rate, cycle time from approval to production, trained staff.
  6. Decisions required — what the board must actually decide.

What should not appear: model counts, pilot counts, or vendor names presented as achievements. Boards that receive activity reporting eventually conclude AI is expensive and unaccountable, and they are not wrong to.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: instrument the baseline before the build
practitioner.text: The single highest-return four weeks in any AI programme are the four weeks spent measuring the current process before anything changes — cycle time, cost per unit, error rate, volume, and the specific decision quality metric that matters. It costs almost nothing, requires no technology, and it is the difference between a defensible business case and an anecdote. Institutions that skip it discover, eighteen months later, that they cannot prove what they achieved.

activity.title: Workplace application
activity.text: For one AI initiative in your institution, construct the four-level value chain: the activity metric, the operational outcome, the business outcome, and the financial outcome — plus the mechanism linking each level to the next. Then stress-test it: is the freed capacity explicitly redirected? Is any of this benefit already claimed by another initiative? If either answer is unsatisfactory, you have found why the business case will not survive.

finance-advanced.title: Leading the AI Transformation in a Nepali Institution
objectives: Synthesise the programme into a coherent institutional strategy
Apply the emerging-market advantage realistically rather than aspirationally
Sequence a credible three-horizon roadmap
Anticipate the specific obstacles Nepali institutions encounter

Complete a defensible enterprise AI strategy for your own institution

sections.h: The strategic position of a Nepali bank
sections.html:
Pull the evidence together honestly.

Working in your favour: the Cambridge finding that EMDE institutions report higher deployment levels than advanced-economy peers; the collapse in entry cost, with 53% of respondents spending under USD 100,000 while reporting high GenAI and agentic maturity; less accumulated legacy technical debt than a two-hundred-year-old European bank; a young, digitally fluent workforce; rapid growth in digital payments generating genuinely valuable behavioural data; and NRB having issued AI Guidelines, which resolves the ambiguity that 79% of regulators globally say they want resolved.

Working against you: scarce specialist talent competing against outbound migration; fragmented core systems and inconsistent customer identifiers; limited local validation capability; dependence on foreign providers with negligible negotiating power; small individual institution scale limiting investment; and thin local evidence, since almost nothing is validated on Nepali populations.

The honest conclusion is that Nepali institutions can reach Scaling maturity within a few years on modest budgets — but only by being disciplined about sequencing, because they cannot afford the expensive parallel experimentation that larger institutions use to find their way.

Horizon 1 — Foundations and credible wins (0–12 months).

  • Compile the model and AI inventory, including AI embedded in purchased software
  • Issue the acceptable-use policy for generative AI and provide an approved alternative tool
  • Establish decision rights, the AI committee, and risk tiering
  • Build the decision inventory (Module 2)
  • Fix entity resolution and the consistent customer identifier
  • Instrument baselines for two or three candidate processes
  • Deliver two internal, low-risk, measurable use cases — document processing, alert prioritisation or an internal policy assistant

Horizon 2 — Decisioning and scale (12–30 months).

  • Stand up shared platform components: feature store, model serving, monitoring, evaluation harness
  • Build independent validation capability, whether internal or contracted
  • Deploy decision-support models with humans deciding — early warning, alert scoring, a credit challenger model
  • Run a first agentic deployment at Level 1 autonomy on a bounded internal process
  • Begin measuring reuse rate and cycle time from approval to production
  • Report AI to the board using the value framework rather than activity counts

Horizon 3 — Business model (30 months onward).

  • Automated decisioning within defined limits, fully governed
  • Personalised propositions and risk-based pricing, fairness-tested
  • New products enabled by AI — the 51% of mature adopters piloting AI-powered products
  • Embedded finance and partner ecosystems
  • Only here does the institution begin crossing from the 86% into the 14%

• Starting with the most exciting use case. Customer-facing generative AI is the most visible and the least forgiving. Earn the right to it.
  • Waiting for core replacement. Build the data layer beside the core (Module 2).
  • Buying a platform before knowing the decisions. The decision inventory should precede the procurement.
  • Hiring data scientists into an institution with no data foundation. They will spend two years on plumbing, become frustrated, and leave — taking the capability with them.
  • Running pilots without baselines. Guarantees an unprovable outcome.
  • Treating governance as a later phase. Retrofitting governance onto deployed systems costs several times more than building it in.

Across every source in this programme, the same behaviours recur among institutions that succeed:

  • Leadership from the top, explicitly. SAS quotes Banorte's Abraham Izquierdo: "Innovation and AI must be recognised as a pillar of the strategy in the institution... leadership from the top is non-negotiable."
  • Business fluency in the AI team — the 40–50% benchmark, and AI leaders who understand banking raising use-case conversion by 20–30%.
  • Honest measurement, including of failures, with baselines instrumented before the build.
  • Willingness to stop projects and to say so publicly.
  • Openness about employment effects rather than allowing rumour to fill the silence.
  • Patience with foundations and impatience with unmeasured activity — most institutions have this precisely backwards.

sections.h: What to do about the evidence gap
sections.html:
A closing point specific to institutions in markets like Nepal. Almost no AI tool sold to you has been validated on a Nepali population. That is a risk, and it is also an opportunity.

The institution that builds genuine local validation capability — the ability to evaluate any model, from any vendor, on its own customers — acquires something that does not depreciate, cannot be bought off the shelf, and improves every subsequent procurement decision. It is the highest-return capability investment available, and it is entirely achievable at modest cost.

Consider also publishing what you learn. The evidence base for AI in South Asian financial populations is thin partly because evaluations conducted here are rarely documented. A well-conducted local validation — including one showing that a tool does not transfer — is a genuine contribution and a reputational asset.

Twelve modules reduce to five propositions:

  1. Adoption is not transformation. 81% are adopting; 14% are transforming. The gap is execution and business integration, and closing it is a board responsibility.
  2. Capability beats use cases. The stack performs at its weakest layer; reuse rate reveals whether you are building or accumulating.
  3. Governance enables scale. The bank that tripled applications without proportional incidents did so because of its framework.
  4. Value must be instrumented before it can be claimed. Baselines first; the efficiency ratio does not lie.
  5. Judgement remains accountable. Explainability, human oversight and named accountability are not constraints on advanced AI — under NRB's framework and every convergent international model, they are its licence to operate.

practitioner.title: Practitioner's note: the twelve-month test
practitioner.text: Whatever strategy you write, apply one test to it: if we execute this perfectly for twelve months, what will be measurably different? If the honest answer is "we will have more pilots and a better understanding," the strategy is a research agenda rather than a plan. A good twelve-month answer names two processes with improved measured outcomes, one governance artefact in operation, and one foundational capability built — modest, specific and defensible.

activity.title: Capstone: your enterprise AI strategy
activity.text: Produce a five-page enterprise AI strategy for your institution containing: (1) an honest maturity assessment against the four-stage ladder with evidence; (2) your weakest capability-stack layer and why; (3) a decision-rights table; (4) a risk-tiered model inventory summary, even if partial; (5) a three-horizon roadmap with named owners and dates; (6) the value framework for your two priority initiatives, with baselines you will instrument; (7) your concentration and dependency assessment; and (8) the twelve-month test — what will be measurably different. This is the deliverable of the programme, and it is written to be presented to your management committee or board.
